{"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "/kind bug

**What happened**:
Trying out snapshot build 20200928 with #3493. virtio-fs is setup to map a cephFS backed PVC.

Ubuntu 18.04. Host kernel: 5.4.0-47-generic. No SELinux. Apparmor enabled.

The `docker-default` AppArmor profile is too restrictive for Virtio-FS to work.

Qemu fails to start with:
```
{"component":"virt-launcher","level":"error","msg":"internal error: qemu unexpectedly closed the monitor: 2020-09-30T21:08:34.249505Z qemu-kvm: -device vhost-user-fs-pci,chardev=chr-vu-fs0,queue-size=1024,tag=sharedfs,bus=pci.1,addr=0x0: Failed to read msg header. Read 0 instead of 12. Original request 1.","pos":"qemuProcessReportLogError:2064","subcomponent":"libvirt","thread":"56","timestamp":"2020-09-30T21:08:34.250000Z"}
qemu-kvm: -device vhost-user-fs-pci,chardev=chr-vu-fs0,queue-size=1024,tag=sharedfs,bus=pci.1,addr=0x0: vhost_dev_init failed: Operation not permitted
```

virtiofsd logs:
```
[617100180193229] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617101334792332] [ID: 00000194] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617101363029043] [ID: 00000194] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617101384956914] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617102539847175] [ID: 00000205] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617102575292582] [ID: 00000205] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617102593016668] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617103827655704] [ID: 00000216] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617103856087607] [ID: 00000216] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617103872973299] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
```

**Workaround**
Annotate the VMI with:
```
      annotations:
        container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/compute: unconfined
```

Since new app armor profiles can't easily be created a reasonable fix to this bug is to have `virt-controller` add this annotation to the Pod. This _might_ fail if AppArmor is enabled in Kubernetes but the kernel module is not loaded. Test on a non-apparmor enabled system before merging a change like this. It should be included in the (hopefully upcoming) documentation for the Virtio-FS implementation at least.", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "This is related to apparmor. I'm wondering what kind of host OS are you testing this on?
Also, there is an additional log file, that is not being collected right now that we can look at.
If you'd exec into the virt-launcher pod `kubectl exec -it [virt-launcher-pod-name] -c compute -n [namespace]` a virtiofsd log file will appear the moment it starts (it may take some time, depending on the infra) - please look in `/var/log/libvirt/qemu/[domain_name]-virtiofsd.log`", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T11:21:05Z", "id": 702067364}, {"author": "person-1118c074", "body": "> This is related to apparmor. I’m running default apparmor settings for Kubernetes / Ubuntu / Docker so I would imagine anyone running Ubuntu on the host will have the same issue as me.", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T12:30:50Z", "id": 702101574}, {"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "Adding `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/compute: unconfined` on the pod spec should solve (or at least workaround) this.", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T18:55:19Z", "id": 702332821}, {"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "@person-1118c074: I have confirmed that annotating the VMI with `unconfined` solves the problem. **Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

> Uncomment only one, leave it on its own line:
>

/kind bug

> /kind enhancement


**What happened**:

The WFFC handling of PVCs right now involves first starting a pod without a VM inside which binds the WFFC PVCs to a node.
Then we hope that when we stop that pod and start the actual pod with a VM inside, that the pod can still fit on the node.

In case that a cluster is used well, this assumption is very likely pretty often false. Also our startup flow is pretty complicated due to that.

Apart from memory and cpu also additional limited resources like devices or hugepages influence how likely it is that a pod can go to the same node again.

**What you expected to happen**:

Instead of using a WFFC pod we should do the following:

 1) record on the VMI status that a DataVolume is used and if it is done with preparataions
 2) record on PVCs if annotations on it indicate that it is a DataVolume
 3) use this status info on the VMI status in virt-handler and virt-launcher to delay timeouts until the import opertions are done
 4) continue with the normal startup flow.

{"author": "person-5bccab16", "body": "Description:
*  There are three components of kubevirt with default installation: kubevirt-handler, kubevirt-controller, kubevirt-api, and kubevirt-operator, the kubevirt-handler is a daemon set running on each node, the controller&api&operator are deployments, each of them is two-pod deployments running on worker nodes randomly.
* There are different cluster roles of these components:
  *  The cluster role of the kubevirt-handler can patch nodes, which can be leveraged to make nodes unschedulable.
  * The cluster role of the kubevirt-controller can create pods/eviction, which can be leveraged to make pods evicted. While the cluster role of kubevirt-api can delete pods, which can be leveraged to make pods recreated and rescheduled to worker nodes.
  * The cluster role of the kubevirt-operator can list all secrets, which can be leveraged to get the admin secret of the entire cluster and make cluster-level privilege escalation.
* If a malicious user controls a worker node, which has kubevirt-handler, and one of kubevirt-api/controller:
  1.  He/she can leverage the kubevirt-handler to path all other nodes with unschedulable: true". And when the kubevirt-operator is rescheduled, the kubevirt-operator will be rescheduled to the malicious worker node.
  2. He/She can use the token of kubevirt-api/controller to evict/delete kubevirt-operator pods, which will be recreated and run on the malicious worker node.
  3. After the kubevirt-operator runs on the malicious worker node, he/she can leverage the operator's token to list all secrets in the whole cluster, get the cluster admin's token and make a cluster-level privilege escalation. 
* Mitigation Discussion:
  *  The cluster role of the kubevirt-operator can use the Resource Names to restrain the secrets which can be listed by the operator itself, however, it may need a careful review of the kubevirt-operator to identify all secrets needed by the operator exactly.
   *  The kubevirt-handler can remove the patch verbs of nodes, and the controller/api can remove the evict and delete of pods. However, similar to the first mitigation, it still needs a careful revisit of the components' source code.
   * The kubevirt can let the kubevirt-operator/controller/api runs on worker nodes (which we called "controller worker node") without running users' workloads, and leverage the isolation of nodes to mitigate the risk. However, if a malicious user leverages some method(i.e., scale-up of kubevirt-handler) and moves to the "controller worker node" horizontally, it still can break the worker nodes' isolation and make privilege escalation.
* Installation and environment:
   * We follow the Kubevirt's [official guide](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/operations/installation/) to install the Kubevirt on a four-node Kubernetes cluster(1.24.2).
I'm looking forward to hearing back from you!

From my POV it is not specifically about k8s credential escalations. The thinking is about workload separation. See answer below.

> My point is: We can lock down virt-handler SA's permissions, and liimt them to a single node. But if we still allow a node to influence other workloads, then an actor on a node, can "simply" try to move workloads to it's own node, until there is a workload with sufficient privileges.
> 

> Thus to me the issue is two fold: Prevent that node can attract workloads, and prevent that workloads can be attracted to a node. It's two sides of the same medal.

Yes we are solving both. But on a different level than what I believe you are suggesting. Like mentioned above already: Attracting workloads is always possible, for instance via just registering your own device plugin and making a desired device available.

The core reason for differntiating between CP and Workers is not necessarily about k8s privileges. It is about separating more privileged components with more required access restrictions from workloads where more people can schedule things.

So: If I have a worker pool, the assumption already is that all the workloads in there have a common risk level. Eventually which node of those gets overtaken is a matter of luck, independent of device and hardware needs. Workloads will kind of randomly land on the compromised node or not. That is at least the mindset one has to have when looking at such a pool when doing risk and security assessments.

This leads then to the following: If I say that my app consists of workload A and workload B, A has more privileges than B, and B is more likely to be taken over (e.g. the public part of an app), I need to ensure that A and B will never scheduled on the same nodes (not even pod antiaffinity, is enough, since a node could have had B already there and be compromised now). You have to create sub-pools based on labels, similar like we do for CP and workloads in k8s.

Bottom line: If you think you can separate apps with different privileges  sufficiently based on some (maybe) existing hardware requirements, there is no sufficient separation in place, and that is not what we have to solve.

What we have to solve is:
 1. CP and worker pool separation can't be compromised by label updates
 2. Separations in any pools, created via labels by users or admins don't get compromised.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe**:
virt launcher pod seems to have velero prehook and posthook annotations by default. Request is to make this optional/configurable or remove it from the virt-launcher pod annotations?
Annotations:
[post.hook.backup.velero.io/command](http://post.hook.backup.velero.io/command): '["/usr/bin/virt-freezer", "--unfreeze", "--name", "centos-stream9-aquamarine-dragon-21", "--namespace", "test-hp-2"]'
    [pre.hook.backup.velero.io/command](http://pre.hook.backup.velero.io/command): '["/usr/bin/virt-freezer", "--freeze", "--name", "centos-stream9-aquamarine-dragon-21", "--namespace", "test-hp-2"]' 
Issue:
If VM is paused, then guest agent commands cannot be run and velero backup would fail.  
If guest agent has permission issues, then guest agent commands and velero backup would fail https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7030558. 

Problem Scenarios:

1. Paused VMs: Guest agent commands cannot execute when VM is paused, causing backup failure.
2. Guest Agent Issues: Permission problems with guest agent result in failed backups.
3. Missing pod for a VM in provisioning state.
4. Any other config issue where velero is not able to run the command in the pod.

**Describe the solution you'd like**:
Requesting removal of this annotation from virt launcher pod.
Backup applications can request prehook and posthook in velerobackup job and also configure onError: Fail or Continue
https://velero.io/docs/main/api-types/backup/

**Describe alternatives you've considered**:
Tried to set prehook and post hook in velero backup job spec but the annotations on the pod took priority. 

**Additional context**:
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

The issue you're experiencing with stale interfaces after an in-place hot-unplug operation in KubeVirt is a known problem. This occurs when the interface added during the hotplug operation is not properly removed during the hot-unplug operation, leaving behind a stale virtual Ethernet (veth) interface in the virt-launcher pod and on the worker node. This issue is specific to in-place hot-unplug operations and does not occur with migration-based hot-unplugs.

The expected behavior is for the hot-unplug operation to clean up any interfaces that were added during the hotplug operation. The logs you provided from the multus and multus-dynamic network controller pods indicate that the removal process was initiated, but the interface was not fully cleaned up.

This issue has been discussed in the KubeVirt community, and there are ongoing efforts to address it. You mentioned that the GitHub issue #13721 might be resolved by pull request #13848, with additional references to pull requests #13941 and #14025. These pull requests may contain fixes or improvements related to the hot-unplug process.

To stay updated on the resolution, you can follow the progress of these pull requests and the associated issue on GitHub. If the problem persists after applying the latest updates, it might be helpful to provide additional logs or context to the maintainers for further investigation. Unfortunately, I didn't find any similar threads that might provide additional insights or solutions.

The issue you're encountering with the Passt binding plugin during the migration test seems to be related to the source VM not having an IPv6 address or routes post-migration. This is crucial for maintaining network connectivity between the VMs.

Here are a few things you might want to check or try:

1. **Passt Binding Plugin Limitations**: The Passt binding plugin is currently in the Alpha stage and has some limitations, such as not supporting custom CIDR configurations in the guest and secondary networks <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/net_binding_plugins/passt)</sup>. These limitations might affect the IPv6 configuration during migration.

2. **Network Configuration**: Ensure that the network configuration for the VMs includes proper IPv6 setup. The Passt plugin should be configured to handle IPv6 addresses and routes correctly. Verify that the `NetworkBindingPlugins` feature gate is enabled in the KubeVirt configuration, as this is necessary for the Passt plugin to function <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/cmd/sidecars/network-passt-binding/README.md)</sup>.

3. **Migration Process**: During migration, KubeVirt should preserve the network configuration, including IPv6 addresses. Check if the migration process is correctly handling the IPv6 setup by ensuring that the `FindMigrationIP` function is retrieving a global unicast IPv6 address for the migration network interface <sup>[[3]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/migration.go)</sup>.

4. **Logs and Debugging**: Check the logs for any error messages or warnings related to the Passt binding plugin during the migration. The Passt log file path is set to `/var/run/kubevirt/passt.log`, which might provide more context on the issue <sup>[[4]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/tests/network/bindingplugin_passt.go)</sup>.

By addressing these areas, you might be able to resolve the issue with the IPv6 configuration during the migration test.

**What happened**:

During peak hours, there was a burst of VMI deletions and creations. With around 2500 VMIs in the cluster, 200 VMIs were deleted and re-created.

This lead to larger vmiCreationToRunning times. Upon investigating, it was found that virt-controller was being slow because of client side rate limiter that needs to get the network-attachment-devices.

This function call is in the critical path of vmiCreationToRunning, because for each vmi, virt-controller looks up the networkMap to render the virt-launcher pod manifest [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/98adfe88a94816a9381c3442372e80e067b98acc/pkg/virt-controller/services/template.go#L375) and [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/98adfe88a94816a9381c3442372e80e067b98acc/pkg/network/multus/nad.go#L64)

virt-controller should to make a cached informer get call to NetworkAttachDefinitions, instead of going to apiserver directly

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
The virt-handler in KubeVirt specifies the cgroup range for Unix98 PTY clients from `c 136:-1` to `c 151:-1` because it includes 16 major numbers starting from 136. This is implemented in the code as follows:

```go
const ptyFirstMajor int64 = 136
const ptyMajors int64 = 16

for i := int64(0); i < ptyMajors; i++ {
    defaultRules = append(defaultRules,
        &devices.Rule{
            Type:        devices.CharDevice,
            Major:       ptyFirstMajor + i,
            Minor:       -1,
            Permissions: permissions,
            Allow:       toAllow,
        })
}
```

This loop iterates 16 times, resulting in the range from 136 to 151. While this differs from the Linux documentation, which specifies the range as `c 136:-1` to `c 143:-1`, the implementation in KubeVirt is consistent with the logic in the code <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/cgroup/util.go)</sup>.

**What happened**:
Machines that does have serial port auto attached and virtualized linux inside opens a getty session on serial port leads to high cpu usage on virt-tail container. Both EFI and BIOS Vms does have this behaviour, so firmware declaration does not appear to change the issue.

**What you expected to happen**:
virt-tail container do not costs about 8% of host CPU per vm

```yaml

kind: VirtualMachine
spec:
  template:
    spec:
        devices:
          autoattachSerialConsole: true
        firmware:
          bootloader:
            bios:
              useSerial: true
```

```

The current configuration sets the CPU request to `5m` and the limit to `15m`. You can modify these values in the `ClusterConfig` to lower the CPU usage:

```go
resources.Requests[k8sv1.ResourceCPU] = resource.MustParse("5m")
resources.Limits[k8sv1.ResourceCPU] = resource.MustParse("15m")
```

Consider reducing these values further if the CPU usage is still high, but ensure that the container has enough resources to function correctly. **What happened**:
CPU set changes, which can occur way later in pod lifecycle (potentially days later)
Can disrupt the block volume hotplug mechanism by reloading the systemd unit
(and thus reverting kubevirt's device allow list for the container)

**What you expected to happen**:
Hotplugged volumes consistently stay accessible in virt launcher
(resync in handler kind of achieves this with a huge delay)

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
This is reproducible in kubevirtci with 2 nodes (cordon ctrl plane for reproducing):
1. Create a non-QoS-Guaranteed VM
2. Hotplug a block PVC into the VM
3. Create a guaranteed pod with 2 CPUs (this will result in a cpuset change for the virt-launcher)
4. Attempt to read from the hotplugged block volume inside the virt launcher
```bash
bash-5.1$ head -c 10 /var/run/kubevirt/hotplug-disks/example-volume-hotplug
head: cannot open '/var/run/kubevirt/hotplug-disks/example-volume-hotplug' for reading: Operation not permitted
```

**Additional context**:
This can be reduced further to issuing a runtime update to the cpu set of the systemd unit
of the virt-launcher. On the node:
```bash
systemctl set-property --runtime crio-17f74e1bdb05666d72672f4cce004416f9232c089921cd12a3a443c4080ba1fa.scope AllowedCPUs=0,3-5
```
Which would reload the unit and revoke access to the block volume in the container, until the next domain resync.

Your observation is correct: when the cpuset for a container changes (such as via a systemd unit reload), the device allow list for the virt-launcher container can be reverted, causing loss of access to block hotplug volumes until the next domain resync. This is a known limitation in how device cgroup rules are managed in KubeVirt.

KubeVirt manages device rules for hotplugged volumes separately from persistent block devices. The relevant logic is in the virt-handler, specifically in functions like `addCurrentRules`, which merges current device rules with new ones to ensure existing rules are preserved if not part of the requested new rules. However, when a systemd unit reload occurs (such as after a cpuset change), the device allow list can be reset, and hotplugged devices may be omitted until the next resync, leading to the "Operation not permitted" error you observed [[source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/cgroup/util.go)].

There is currently no upstream documentation or code change that directly addresses this race between cpuset changes and device rule persistence for hotplugged block volumes. The only built-in mitigation is the periodic resync in the handler, which, as you noted, can take a significant amount of time to restore access.

Workarounds or mitigations you might consider:
- Trigger a manual resync or restart of the virt-handler to expedite restoration of device rules.
- Avoid runtime cpuset changes for virt-launcher containers with hotplugged block volumes, if possible.
- If you have control over the systemd or container runtime configuration, investigate ways to persist or re-apply device cgroup rules after cpuset changes, though this is not natively handled by KubeVirt at this time.

If you are looking for a more robust solution, it would likely require changes in how KubeVirt tracks and reapplies device allow lists after systemd or runtime property changes. This is an area that may need further upstream attention.

For more details on how hotplug volumes and device rules are managed, see the relevant code in [`pkg/virt-handler/cgroup/util.go`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/cgroup/util.go) and the [hotplug volumes documentation](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/operations/hotplug_volumes).

If you need more technical details or want to discuss possible design changes, let me know.

The tolerations you set in the KubeVirt CR under `spec.workloads.nodePlacement` only apply to KubeVirt infrastructure components (like virt-handler), not to VirtualMachineInstances (VMIs) themselves. This means that even if you configure tolerations in the KubeVirt CR, new VMIs will not automatically inherit those tolerations. To allow VMIs to be scheduled on nodes with taints such as `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` or `node-role.kubernetes.io/etcd`, you must explicitly add the required tolerations to each VMI or VirtualMachine spec under `spec.template.spec.tolerations` [reference](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/node_assignment).

This design is intentional: KubeVirt separates infrastructure placement from VMI placement, so there is no implicit inheritance of tolerations from the operator-level configuration to VMIs [reference](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/7ecefcee556034b4601b08554bb7e7ce3ca98f9f/staging/src/kubevirt.io/api/core/v1/types.go). The only way to ensure VMIs tolerate specific taints is to set the tolerations directly in the VMI or VirtualMachine manifest.

If you want all VMIs to tolerate certain taints by default, you will need to ensure every VMI or VirtualMachine spec includes those tolerations. There is currently no cluster-level or webhook mechanism in KubeVirt that automatically injects tolerations from the KubeVirt CR into VMIs [reference](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/7ecefcee556034b4601b08554bb7e7ce3ca98f9f/pkg/virt-controller/services/template.go).

If you already added tolerations to the VMI spec and the VM still avoids the control-plane nodes, double-check that the tolerations are present in the running pod spec (e.g., with `kubectl get pod <virt-launcher-pod> -o yaml`). If the tolerations are missing, verify your VirtualMachine or VMI manifest syntax.

There are no known bugs or limitations in KubeVirt v1.5.1 regarding this behavior. This is the expected and documented scheduling model.

The documentation line you quoted—"The placement of the virt-handler DaemonSet pods (and consequently, the placement of the VM workloads scheduled to the cluster) is governed by the .spec.workloads.nodePlacement field in the KubeVirt CR"—can definitely be read as implying that VM workloads will inherit nodePlacement settings from the KubeVirt CR. However, in practice, KubeVirt intentionally separates the placement configuration for its infrastructure components (like virt-handler) from the scheduling configuration for VirtualMachineInstances (VMIs).

Here's how it works:

- The `.spec.workloads.nodePlacement` field in the KubeVirt CR only affects the placement of the virt-handler DaemonSet pods themselves—not the VMIs. This means you can control which nodes run virt-handler, but this does not automatically allow VMIs to be scheduled on those nodes.
- VMIs (and VMs) require their own tolerations and node selectors to be set explicitly in their manifests. There is no inheritance or automatic propagation of tolerations from the KubeVirt CR to VMIs. This is confirmed in the [KubeVirt node assignment documentation](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/node_assignment), which states that tolerations must be applied directly to VMs to allow them to schedule onto tainted nodes.

The rationale for this design is to give cluster administrators fine-grained control: you might want to run virt-handler on certain nodes for operational reasons (for example, to monitor or manage nodes that are not intended to run workloads), but only allow VM workloads on a subset of those nodes. This separation avoids accidental scheduling of VMs onto nodes that should only host infrastructure components.

If your goal is to allow VMs to run "anywhere possible," you need to ensure that each VM or VMI manifest includes the necessary tolerations for all taints present on your nodes. There is currently no cluster-wide default or webhook to inject these tolerations automatically into every VM or VMI. This has been discussed in the community, especially in the context of clusters like Rancher RKE2, where additional taints (like `node-role.kubernetes.io/etcd`) are common and can block scheduling if not explicitly tolerated by the VM spec ([discussion](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14429)).

So, while the documentation could be clearer, the current behavior is by design: virt-handler placement and VM workload placement are configured independently. If you want VMs to run on all nodes where virt-handler is present, you must add the appropriate tolerations to your VM or VMI specs.

**What happened**:

I imported the `kubevirt.io/client-go` into my project that is using recent `k8s.io/*` libaries (`>= 0.34.0`) which made `go mod tidy` fail with warnings about the NetworkingV1Alpha1 API missing.

**What you expected to happen**:

The imported client should work in projects using recent `k8s.io/*` libaries (`>= 0.34.0`).

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Import `kubevirt.io/client-go` with `v1.6.0` into project using recent `k8s.io/*` libaries (`>= 0.34.0`) and run `go mod tidy`.

**Additional context**:

Dropping the mocked client (`kubecli/generated_mock_kubevirt.go` and `‎kubecli/kubevirt_test_utils.go` allows to drop the dependency on the NetworkingV1Alpha1 API which is not present in the latest `k8s.io/api` and other `k8s.io/*` package versions.

See for example https://github.com/person-f36cb5b0/kubevirt-client-go/commit/0de0a14ecd487cd01cede0b72bf6ad640c9d0a3f.

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): N/A
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): N/A
- VM or VMI specifications: N/A
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): N/A
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): N/A
- Install tools: N/A
- Others: N/A

The reason `go mod tidy` fails when importing `kubevirt.io/client-go` with recent `k8s.io/*` libraries (>= 0.34.0) is that the published `client-go` module includes mocked client files (`generated_mock_kubevirt.go` and `kubevirt_test_utils.go`) that import deprecated Kubernetes API packages like `networking/v1alpha1` and `coordination/v1alpha1`, which have been removed from recent Kubernetes releases. This causes dependency resolution to fail when those APIs are missing in the newer `k8s.io` modules [[source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14819)].

These mocked client files are intended for testing but are included in the main module and not separated out, so any consumer of `kubevirt.io/client-go` inherits these problematic dependencies. There are currently no merged PRs or official workarounds to resolve this, and the maintainers have acknowledged the issue but have not yet refactored the packaging to exclude these mocks from the published module [[source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14819)].

Users have tried regenerating the mocks to remove references to removed APIs, but this is not officially supported and may not be reliable. There is no official documentation or guidance on this issue in the KubeVirt user guide or release notes.

At this time, there is no supported way to use `kubevirt.io/client-go` with recent `k8s.io/*` libraries without encountering this problem. The only reliable solution would be for the maintainers to refactor the module to keep mocks and test helpers out of the main export, following Go best practices. For now, you may need to consider workarounds like forking the module and removing the mock files yourself, but this is not officially recommended or supported [[source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14819)].

**What happened**:
When a hot-pluggable resource is changed (e.g. a CPU socket), VMs managed by a VirtualMachinePool receive a `HotVCPUChange` condition, but the VMI is are replaced anyway instead of live migrating.

**What you expected to happen**:
Updating hot-pluggable resources on VMs managed by a vmpool should not get restarted.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Deploy a vmpool. From the docs, with only `spec.virtualMachineTemplate.spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.sockets` added:

    ```yaml
    apiVersion: pool.kubevirt.io/v1alpha1
    kind: VirtualMachinePool
    metadata:
      name: vm-pool-cirros
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          kubevirt.io/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
      virtualMachineTemplate:
        metadata:
          creationTimestamp: null
          labels:
            kubevirt.io/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
        spec:
          runStrategy: Always
          template:
            metadata:
              creationTimestamp: null
              labels:
                kubevirt.io/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
            spec:
              domain:
                cpu:
                  sockets: 1
                devices:
                  disks:
                  - disk:
                      bus: virtio
                    name: containerdisk
                resources:
                  requests:
                    memory: 128Mi
              terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
              volumes:
              - containerDisk:
                  image: kubevirt/cirros-container-disk-demo:latest
                name: containerdisk
    ````
2. Change a hot-plugable field:

    ```shell
    kubectl patch vmpool vm-pool-cirros --type='json' -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/virtualMachineTemplate/spec/template/spec/domain/cpu/sockets", "value": 2}]'
    ```
3. Check the VM's conditions:

    ```console
    $ kubectl get vm vm-pool-cirros-0 -o json | jq '.status.conditions[] | select(.type == "HotVCPUChange")'
    {
      "lastProbeTime": null,
      "lastTransitionTime": null,
      "status": "True",
      "type": "HotVCPUChange"
    }
    ```
4. Observe the pod being deleted:

    ```console
    $ kubectl get pod virt-launcher-vm-pool-cirros-0-b6ptv -o json | jq '.metadata.deletionTimestamp'
    "2025-10-23T05:26:50Z"
    ```

**Additional context**:
I am guessing that this is due to the selector being updated but I'm not 100% sure

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): v1.6.2
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.33.4
- VM or VMI specifications: See above
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): N/A

- Others: N/A
", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This behavior is expected in KubeVirt as of v1.6.2. When you update hot-pluggable resources like CPU sockets in a VirtualMachinePool, the pool controller reconciles the VM spec to match the template. If the change can't be applied live (for example, if it exceeds the allowed hotplug limits or the platform doesn't support live hotplug), the VM receives a `HotVCPUChange` condition, and the controller sets a `RestartRequired` condition, which triggers a VM restart and pod replacement instead of a live migration. This logic applies to both standalone VMs and those managed by pools—there's no special handling in pools to avoid restarts for these changes. The restart is not caused by the selector update, but by the pool's reconciliation and the underlying VM controller logic. For more details, see the [controller code](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/vm.go) and [user guide](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/user_workloads/instancetypes/#hotplug).

If you want to avoid restarts, make sure your changes meet the hotplug requirements (such as not exceeding `MaxSockets` and using supported architectures). Otherwise, a restart will be required for the changes to take effect.

You're right—this is a VirtualMachinePool-specific limitation. When you update a hotpluggable resource like CPU sockets on a VM managed by a pool, the pool controller enforces strict alignment between the VM spec and the pool template. Even if the change is hotpluggable and would work live for a standalone VM, the pool's reconciliation logic will delete and recreate the VM to match the template revision, rather than attempting a live hotplug update. This is intentional and represents a fundamental difference between standalone and pool-managed VMs in KubeVirt as of v1.6.2. There is currently no special handling in the pool controller to leverage live hotplug for these updates, so restarts are expected in this scenario—even when all hotplug requirements are met. For more details, see the pool controller logic and update strategy discussion [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14073) and [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-controller/watch/pool/pool.go).

This is a known issue in KubeVirt v1.6.0: the guest-console-log (guest-os-console) container was refactored to run as a sidecar with its own restart policy, but if it can't find the logfile `/var/run/kubevirt-private/<id>/virt-serial0-log` (often due to timing/race conditions during pod startup), it fails and can cause the pod to get stuck at init status. This is more likely with complex network setups or multiple NADs, which delay log file creation [details](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15134).

A Kubernetes v1.34 change in pod condition handling also caused patch requests from virt-controller to fail, impacting pod initialization and guest-console-log readiness in v1.6.0. This was fixed by [PR #15599](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15599)—upgrading to a newer KubeVirt release with this fix should resolve the stuck pod issue [reference](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15586).

If you want to avoid guest-console-log failures impacting readiness, you can disable serial console logging by setting `vmi.Spec.Domain.Devices.AutoattachSerialConsole: false` or globally via the KubeVirt CR with `spec.configuration.virtualMachineOptions.disableSerialConsoleLog` [reference](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15501).

The log file is created by the virt-launcher (compute) container, and the VM itself will continue running even if guest-console-log fails. For more on the underlying race/timing issue and workarounds, see [this discussion](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15134).

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
The missing mount for `kubevirt-virt-handler-certs` in the virt-handler DaemonSet is due to changes in KubeVirt v1.7.0: new migration and vsock client certificates were introduced and are now mounted, but the operator stopped mounting the original client certificate, even though the code still tries to load it. This appears to be an oversight or incomplete migration in the operator logic, not an intentional removal, since the secret is still created and referenced in the code but not mounted in the pod [source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16168).

The client certificate at `/etc/virt-handler/clientcertificates/tls.crt` is used for outgoing mTLS connections from virt-handler, for example, when it needs to prove its identity to other components. Its absence could impact any flows that still rely on this certificate, though most migration and vsock features now use their dedicated certificates [source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/b84d8ce53de7d36f99dd31c14f3f956ab308c269/cmd/virt-handler/virt-handler.go#L122-L751).

If you need to suppress the error or restore any legacy functionality, you can manually patch the DaemonSet to mount the missing secret at `/etc/virt-handler/clientcertificates`. Otherwise, monitor for issues in migration or secure communication between components—if you see failures, restoring the mount may help. This is likely a bug and may be resolved in future releases.

This is a known limitation after a QEMU version upgrade in KubeVirt: when you upgrade from KubeVirt 1.6.2 (QEMU 9.1.0-19.el9) to 1.7 (QEMU 9.1.0-20.el9), live migration of VMs that were running before the upgrade can fail with errors like "Failed to load virtio-net" and "Operation not permitted". This happens because the in-memory state of a running VM is tied to the QEMU version it started with, and after the upgrade, the new QEMU can't always interpret the old state, especially for devices like virtio-net. This is not specific to your network configuration or CNI plugin.

Restarting the affected VMs after the upgrade reinitializes their state with the new QEMU version, which resolves the migration issue. New VMs started after the upgrade are also unaffected. There is no automated workaround in KubeVirt for this scenario, and it's not currently documented in the release notes or user guide [[source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15474)].

To mitigate: after upgrading KubeVirt and QEMU, restart all running VMs before attempting live migration.

If you have further questions or need help with related troubleshooting, let me know!

The root cause is a downstream QEMU patch in `qemu-kvm-9.1.0-20.el9` that retroactively disables **USO (UDP Segmentation Offload)** features on RHEL 9 machine types, breaking live migration from `qemu-kvm-9.1.0-19.el9`.

### The QEMU change

In `qemu-kvm-9.1.0-20.el9`, the patch `kvm-virtio-net-disable-USO-for-virt-rhel9.6.patch` was added, tracked under [RHEL-80313](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/RHEL-80313) ("Unable to migrate VM from RHEL10.0/qemu-kvm-9.6 to RHEL9.6/qemu-kvm-9.6"). The intent was to fix migration from RHEL 10 to RHEL 9 by disabling USO on RHEL 9 machine types. The side effect is that VMs already running on `9.1.0-19` (where USO was enabled and negotiated with the guest) can no longer migrate to `9.1.0-20` (where USO is now disallowed).

The commit range is visible at https://gitlab.com/redhat/centos-stream/rpms/qemu-kvm/-/compare/52929cc8...609fe233.

### Feature bitmap breakdown

The error `Features 0x1c0010130afffaf unsupported. Allowed features: 0x10179bfffef` corresponds to three migration-breaking virtio-net feature bits that are set in the source VM but rejected by the target QEMU:

| Bit | Flag | Description |
|-----|------|-------------|
| 54 | `VIRTIO_NET_F_GUEST_USO4` | Guest can receive USOv4 |
| 55 | `VIRTIO_NET_F_GUEST_USO6` | Guest can receive USOv6 |
| 56 | `VIRTIO_NET_F_HOST_USO` | Host can send USO |

VMs started on `9.1.0-19` negotiated these USO features with the guest kernel. When migrating to `9.1.0-20`, QEMU validates the incoming virtio-net device state against its (now reduced) allowed feature set and rejects it.

### Why KubeVirt amplifies the problem

Several aspects of KubeVirt's upgrade flow make this worse:

1. **Target virt-launcher always uses the new image** - during migration the target pod is rendered with the current (new) virt-launcher image, meaning it always runs the new QEMU. There is no mechanism to pin the old QEMU for in-flight migrations.
2. **`workloadUpdateMethods: [LiveMigrate]` triggers migrations automatically** - the workload updater detects outdated `LauncherContainerImageVersion` and creates migrations for all running VMs, hitting every VM at once.
3. **No preflight capability check** - KubeVirt does not compare virtio-net (or other device) feature bitmaps between source and target QEMU before starting a migration. It relies on libvirt/QEMU to validate at migration time.
4. **No feature filtering in migration XML** - the pre-migration hooks adjust CPU topology and network config but do not filter device-level feature bits.

### Why new/restarted VMs work fine

A VM started or restarted on `9.1.0-20` negotiates features against the new QEMU, which no longer offers USO. The guest never enables those bits, so subsequent migrations succeed.

### Summary

This is a stable guest ABI violation in downstream QEMU packaging: USO features were available and negotiated by guests, then a later patch retroactively removed them without a migration-compatible transition. - Kubernetes cluster running **KubeVirt v1.6.3** (any small number of running VMs reproduces — we hit it on a 6-VM dev cluster and again on production with 161).

1. Upgrade KubeVirt to **v1.8.2**, skipping v1.7.x. We're skipping 1.7 because it's blocked by this same issue, so users who lag a release fall straight into a 1.6 → 1.8 jump.
2. Leave `workloadUpdateStrategy.workloadUpdateMethods: [LiveMigrate, Evict]` at defaults.
3. Once `observedKubeVirtVersion: v1.8.2`, virt-controller starts scheduling `kubevirt-evacuation-*` migrations for every still-running v1.6.3 launcher pod.

Every live-migration fails. Phase transitions look healthy through `TargetReady → Running`, then explode at libvirt's `migration in`:

The upgrade test in `tests/operator/operator.go` (`from previous release to target tested release`, ~L653) **does** start VMs on the previous release, upgrade KubeVirt, and verify live-migration. One thing that might explain why the regression slipped through:

Sorted by realism. (1) and (2) are KubeVirt-side; (3) is per-cluster mitigation that would let us roll out the fix today.

1. **`workloadUpdateMethod: Restart`.** New strategy alongside `LiveMigrate`/`Evict` that explicitly cold-restarts the VM (stop + start through the VM controller, bypassing the eviction interceptor webhook). {"author": "person-0d5c74a9", "body": "**What happened**:
Was able to create a KubeVirt CR with spec.infra.replicas == 0

**What you expected to happen**:
It should have failed just like it does on update.
This problem most likely exists on all other validated spec fields!

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Create a KubeVirt CR with forbidden values (which would fail update validation)
", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This is a known gap in KubeVirt: the create admission webhook only validates the schema and checks for an existing KubeVirt CR, but does not perform semantic validation of spec fields (like infra.replicas > 0) on creation. All detailed spec validation—including checks for infra.replicas, node placement, TLS/cert rules, seccomp, and others—happens only in the update admission webhook. That’s why you can create a CR with forbidden values, but updates with those values are rejected. The code even includes a TODO about this missing validation on creation, but there’s no open issue or PR tracking a fix right now. This means any field validated in the update webhook is affected, not just infra.replicas. If you need to enforce these constraints on creation, you’ll need to pre-validate your specs before submitting them, or consider contributing to extend the create webhook to include semantic validation.  
[Reference: kubevirt-create-admitter.go](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/920545416cea9b30a057c693c3313312dbb36e34/pkg/virt-operator/webhooks/kubevirt-create-admitter.go#L49-L71) | [Reference: kubevirt-update-admitter.go](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/920545416cea9b30a057c693c3313312dbb36e34/pkg/virt-operator/webhooks/kubevirt-update-admitter.go#L66-L435)

**What happened**:
If pod IP does not exist in VMI interface status, the IP from guest agent (if present) is written to the status. 
So in a dual stack or single IPv4 stack environment if pod IP does not exist and internal IP addresses are still configured on the guest VM (though dhcp/ipam etc maybe), they are shown on the interface status even though they are not reachable.

**What you expected to happen**:
In dual stack or single IPv4 stack environments only the pod IP should appear on the interface status.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Create a VM with masquerade binding without a pod IP in a single ipv4/6 or dual stack environment.
Configure an IPv4 private IP manually or through cloudinit on the guest VM.
Check the VMI interface status for this IP.

**Additional context**:
The [e2e test](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/5bcc0285422e0cb7f2918bc9907d676a5f0b342f/tests/network/networkpolicy.go#L123) that verifies connectivity between 2 masquerage VMs does not catch this as of now. The IPs configured on the server and client VMs [through cloudinit](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/988472e0fef5c66e0ee5df43a07f0fc231a4b2c3/tests/libnet/cloudinit/cloudinit.go#L183) are the same. So if the client VM pings the server IP, and even if this server IP is not reachable, it essentially pings itself and passes.

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): N/A
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): N/A
- VM or VMI specifications: N/A
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): N/A
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): N/A
- Install tools: N/A
- Others: N/A
", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-a2c0ed82", "body": "/sig network", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-12-29T10:53:23Z", "id": 3696157981}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This is a known behavior in KubeVirt: when using masquerade binding, if the pod IP is missing, the VMI interface status may include IPs reported by the guest agent—even if those IPs are private or unreachable from outside the VM. Currently, only Link Local Addresses (LLAs) (e.g., `fe80::/10` for IPv6, `169.254.0.0/16` for IPv4) are filtered out for masquerade interfaces to avoid exposing obviously unusable addresses [[PR #16242](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16242)]. Other private or unreachable guest-configured IPs are not filtered and may still appear if the pod IP is absent.

There is no configuration option or best practice to restrict the interface status to only pod IPs for masquerade binding. The filtering is limited to LLAs in code, and tests only ensure that pod IPs are present (not that extra IPs are excluded) [[PR #15776](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15776)]. A recent change also limits the number of guest agent interfaces reported to avoid status bloat, but this does not affect which IPs are shown [[PR #16391](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16391)].

If you need stricter filtering (e.g., only pod IPs in status), you would need to extend the filtering logic in the virt-handler's network status update code (see `ifacesStatusFromGuestAgent` in `pkg/network/setup/netstat.go`). As a workaround, you can ignore guest agent IPs in your client logic or monitor for future KubeVirt updates that might address this more comprehensively.

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This is a known issue in KubeVirt. The duplicate SR-IOV interface entries in VMI status happen because the merging logic can't correlate the guest-agent's report (which has the MAC and interface name) with the domain/multus-status report (which has the network name and PodInterfaceName but may lack the MAC/IP). This usually occurs when the guest agent doesn't report the MAC address, so KubeVirt treats the guest-agent interface as a separate entry instead of merging them into one. The InfoSource field shows which sources contributed data to each entry—ideally, you'd see a single entry with all sources listed, but when correlation fails, you get two entries describing the same interface with different attributes [PR 16411](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16411).

This is not expected behavior, but it's a known and tested scenario. There is no documented configuration option or workaround to force deduplication in the user guide [user guide](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/interfaces_and_networks/). Setting an explicit MAC address in your VMI spec can help the merging logic correlate the entries and produce a single interface status entry [PR 16411](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16411).

Timing issues (like delays in the downward API file population or guest-agent reporting) can make this worse, especially during migration or under cluster load. Increasing assertion timeouts in tests and ensuring all components (Multus, SR-IOV device plugin) are ready before VM launch can help with test flakiness but won't directly solve the duplicate entry issue [issue 13648](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/13648).

For more details, see:
- [PR 16411 discussion](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16411)
- [KubeVirt user guide: interfaces and networks](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/interfaces_and_networks/)
- [Issue 13648: SR-IOV VMI interface status flakiness](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/13648)

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
You can update the CDI version used for testing on the release-1.6 branch by bumping the kubevirtci SHA referenced in that branch. Even though kubevirtci itself isn't branched, the version of CDI it deploys is determined by the kubevirtci SHA you point to. Recent merged PRs (like [#15456](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15456) and [#15507](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15507)) updated the kubevirtci SHA in release-1.6 to deploy CDI v1.63.0 via gocli, using the `KUBEVIRT_CUSTOM_CDI_VERSION` environment variable (which now defaults to v1.63.0). So, to ensure you're testing against CDI >=v1.63.0, just make sure your release-1.6 branch references a kubevirtci SHA that includes this bump.

{"author": "person-05387dcb", "body": "**Note**: This bug tracks the **long-term architectural fix** to establish and enforce a consistent synchronizer interface contract. See #16496 for the short-term, backportable fix for immediate ResourceVersion conflicts.

**What happened**:
The synchronizer interface implementations are inconsistent in how they interact with the Kubernetes API. Some synchronizers make direct API calls (`Patch()`, `Update()`, `PatchStatus()`, `UpdateStatus()`), while others only modify the local VM object and rely on the main VM controller to persist changes. This architectural inconsistency leads to:

1. **ResourceVersion conflicts**: When synchronizers make direct API calls but don't properly propagate the updated ResourceVersion back through the call chain
2. **Unexpected behavior**: The main VM sync loop expects synchronizers to only modify the local object, not make API calls
3. **Difficult to reason about**: Multiple code paths can update the same VM object via different API call patterns
4. **Hard to maintain**: No clear contract for what synchronizer implementations should and shouldn't do

**Current state of synchronizer implementations**:

- **Network Synchronizer** (`pkg/network/controllers/vm.go:70-108`):
  - ✅ Does NOT make direct VM API calls
  - Only modifies local VM copy and returns it
  - (Does patch the VMI at lines 140-142, but that's a different resource)
  - **This is the ideal pattern**

- **Firmware Synchronizer** (`pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/firmware.go:48-81`):
  - ❌ DOES make direct VM API calls
  - Calls `Patch()` on the VM Spec at line 78-80
  - Returns the updated VM from the API response
  - Properly propagates ResourceVersion, but violates the ideal synchronizer pattern

- **Instancetype Synchronizer** (`pkg/instancetype/controller/vm/controller.go:114-217`):
  - ❌ DOES make direct VM API calls in multiple places:
    - `Store()` flow calls `PatchStatus()` at `pkg/instancetype/revision/patch.go:43` (discards response)
    - `Upgrade()` flow calls `PatchStatus()` at `pkg/instancetype/upgrade/handler.go:81` (discards response)
    - `Expand()` flow calls `Update()` and `UpdateStatus()` at lines 185-195
  - Inconsistent about capturing and returning API responses
  - **Has the most violations and the most issues**

**What you expected to happen**:

All synchronizer implementations should follow a consistent contract:

1. **No direct API calls**: Synchronizers should NOT call `Patch()`, `Update()`, `PatchStatus()`, or `UpdateStatus()` on the VM object
2. **Local modifications only**: Synchronizers should only modify the local `vm` object passed to them (both Spec and Status fields are allowed)
3. **Return modified object**: Return the modified VM object and let the main VM controller detect changes and persist them
4. **The main VM controller is responsible for persistence**: The VM sync loop should detect what changed and make appropriate API calls

This contract should be:
- Documented clearly in the synchronizer interface
- Enforced through code reviews
- Potentially enforced through testing or linting

**How to reproduce the architectural inconsistency**:

1. Review `pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/vm.go:236-238` - the synchronizer interface definition has no documentation
2. Review the three synchronizer implementations listed above
3. Observe that they have completely different patterns for API interaction
4. Note that the VM sync loop at `vm.go:3001-3006` expects synchronizers to modify Spec but doesn't handle Status changes properly
5. Observe that there's no clear guidance on what synchronizers should do

**Long-term fix (architectural)**:

1. **Document the synchronizer interface contract**:
   ```go
   // synchronizer defines the contract for VM synchronizers.
   // Implementations MUST:
   // - Only modify the local vm object (both Spec and Status fields are allowed)
   // - NOT make direct API calls (Patch, Update, PatchStatus, UpdateStatus) on the VM
   // - Return the modified VM object
   // The main VM controller is responsible for detecting changes and persisting them.
   type synchronizer interface {
       Sync(*virtv1.VirtualMachine, *virtv1.VirtualMachineInstance) (*virtv1.VirtualMachine, error)
   }
   ```

You're right about the architectural inconsistency: the synchronizer interface in KubeVirt is currently undocumented and not consistently enforced. The main VM controller expects synchronizers to only modify the local VM object and return it, leaving all persistence (API calls) to the controller itself. This pattern is followed by the network synchronizer, which only updates the local copy and never calls the API directly ([source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/55c46da55cdf98eccb15745d20cb92d976fcc42e/pkg/network/controllers/vm.go#L70-L142)). In contrast, both the firmware and instancetype synchronizers make direct API calls to update or patch the VM object, violating the intended contract and causing the issues you described ([firmware](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/55c46da55cdf98eccb15745d20cb92d976fcc42e/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/firmware.go#L48-L81), [instancetype](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/55c46da55cdf98eccb15745d20cb92d976fcc42e/pkg/instancetype/controller/vm/controller.go#L114-L216)).

The ideal contract for synchronizers should be:

- Do not make direct API calls (Patch, Update, PatchStatus, UpdateStatus) on the VM object.
- Only modify the local VM object (Spec and Status are both allowed).
- Return the modified VM object; let the main VM controller detect and persist changes.

Currently, the main VM controller's sync loop runs all synchronizers on a local VM copy, then persists changes to Spec/Metadata via a single Update() call and Status via a separate UpdateStatus() call, based on DeepEqual comparisons to the original VM object ([source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/55c46da55cdf98eccb15745d20cb92d976fcc42e/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/vm.go#L270-L3272)). This means any synchronizer that makes its own API calls can break assumptions, leading to ResourceVersion conflicts and hard-to-debug behavior.

To address this, you should:

1. Document the synchronizer interface contract directly in the code.
2. Refactor the firmware and instancetype synchronizers to only modify the local VM object and never make direct API calls.
3. Update the VM sync loop to detect and persist both Spec and Status changes after all synchronizers run.
4. Add tests (with a mocked client) to ensure synchronizers do not make API calls during Sync.

This approach will make the codebase easier to reason about, reduce ResourceVersion conflicts, and improve maintainability and testability. There are no other synchronizer implementations currently wired into the VM controller, so only the network, firmware, and instancetype synchronizers need to be addressed at this time ([source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/55c46da55cdf98eccb15745d20cb92d976fcc42e/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vm/vm.go#L270-L3272)).

Hi @person-1694c7d8! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
This timeout happens because SyncVirtualMachine calls into virt-launcher, which in turn calls libvirt's GetBlockInfo synchronously to retrieve disk info. If the guest is doing heavy disk IO, this libvirt call can block for a long time, causing the whole SyncVirtualMachine operation to hang until the outer 20s gRPC timeout is hit. When that happens, the VMI gets marked Synchronized=False. There are no retries, non-blocking mechanisms, or configuration options to adjust this timeout or to skip the GetBlockInfo call under heavy IO—it's a hardcoded behavior in the current KubeVirt implementation. The domain lock is held during this process, so other management operations can also be blocked while waiting for disk info to return. No official workarounds or best practices are documented for this scenario, and this limitation is not addressed in the user guide or blogs. The only mitigation right now is to avoid sustained heavy disk IO in the guest if you need reliable management operations, or to consider reporting this as a feature gap if it critically impacts your use case.  
[Reference: code analysis and related issues](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/manager.go#L1137-L1605)

This bug is caused by a race condition during KubeVirt upgrades: the install-strategy job generates the new install strategy ConfigMap by running virt-operator with --dump-install-strategy, but it only includes ServiceMonitor and PrometheusRule resources if it can find the monitoring ServiceAccount at that exact moment. If the ServiceAccount isn't present (often due to timing during upgrades), the configmap is created without ServiceMonitor, and VM metrics are no longer scraped. There is no retry or wait logic, so the omission persists until the configmap is manually regenerated after the monitoring resources are available. Manually triggering virt-operator to regenerate the configmap restores metrics, confirming this timing issue. No upstream fix or official workaround exists beyond manual regeneration, and no open issues in the KubeVirt repo directly track this bug. Explicitly setting serviceMonitorNamespace in the KubeVirt config ensures ServiceMonitor is created, but doesn't address the race during upgrades. Fresh installs are less likely to hit this because the monitoring ServiceAccount usually exists before the job runs.  
[Reference: strategy.go logic](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-operator/resource/generate/install/strategy.go#L273-L634)

	oldLabels := vmi.Labels

This is a known issue in KubeVirt 1.6.2: after live migration, there can be a window where both source and target virt-launcher pods are running for the same VM, which can lead to corruption if both remain active. The migration proxy is shut down immediately after migration completion, but pod termination is delayed until the cluster reconciles the VMI's node assignment. This race condition is documented in [issue #15373](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15373) and related threads.

While PRs #15721 and #15766 addressed the main bug in 1.6.2, some users still report rare cases where the source pod fails to shut down, especially under heavy migration load. A grpc client closure race in the migration finalization logic can also interfere with proper cleanup, as described in [issue #16557](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16557). This was fixed in KubeVirt 1.7+ ([PR #16022](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16022)).

If you encounter duplicate virt-launcher pods after migration, the safest mitigation is to manually delete the older pod to prevent VM corruption. For 1.6.2, you can patch the code so that `CloseLauncherClient` is only called after `SignalTargetPodCleanup` in the failure path, which helps avoid the grpc client race ([details](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16557)). The long-term solution is to upgrade to KubeVirt 1.7+.

For more details and troubleshooting, see:
- [Issue #15373](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/15373)
- [Issue #16557](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16557)
- [Migration lifecycle docs](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/live_migration/)

Hi @person-65aa7e61! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a known behavior in KubeVirt: when any disk—including secret volumes like the ACPI MSDM table—is slow or unresponsive due to I/O contention, the VM will pause with an I/O error. This is the default and currently unchangeable behavior for secret volumes; the errorPolicy field (which can make the VM report errors in the guest instead of pausing) is not supported for disks created from secrets, including the MSDM disk. There are no documented workarounds or best practices specific to secret volumes under heavy disk load, and the only general mitigation is to reduce I/O contention—for example, by isolating critical disks on separate physical devices or using IOThreads for high-I/O disks (though IOThreads cannot be assigned to secret disks) [[docs](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/storage/disks_and_volumes/)].

This area is under active discussion and testing in the community, but as of now, the VM pause on I/O error for secret volumes is hardcoded and cannot be configured away via the VM spec [[issue](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14589)] [[docs](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/storage/disks_and_volumes/)]. If this is a blocker, you may want to track ongoing work to improve error handling and disk I/O reliability in KubeVirt.

{"author": "person-a141d187", "body": "
**What happened:**
After migrating a Windows VM from VMware into KubeVirt using CDI/v2v (DataVolumeTemplates), the VM only boots successfully on the first boot when the boot disk bus is sata.

If the VM is created to boot with virtio or scsi (virtio-scsi controller) on the first boot, it fails to boot.
However, once the VM has booted successfully at least once using SATA, we can patch the VM disk bus to virtio or scsi and reboot, and then it boots successfully with those buses.

In other words: virtio/scsi work only after an initial SATA boot, even though the Windows guest had virtio drivers installed pre-migration in VMware.

**What you expected to happen:**
The migrated Windows VM should be able to boot on the first boot with the boot disk bus set to virtio or scsi (virtio-scsi), especially if virtio drivers were installed in the guest prior to migration. SATA should not be required as a “first boot staging” workaround.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. Take an existing Windows VM in VMware vCenter and ensure it is powered off. (Virtio drivers are installed in-guest pre-migration.)
2. Migrate/import the VM into KubeVirt using CDI/v2v (VMware → DataVolumeTemplates workflow).
3. Create a KubeVirt VirtualMachine that references the imported DataVolumes.
4. Set the boot disk bus to virtio (or scsi) before the first boot. Example JSON patch used in our automation:
5. (Similarly reproduced with "value": "scsi" with a virtio-scsi controller.)
`
[
  {
    "op": "replace",
    "path": "/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/disks/0/disk/bus",
    "value": "virtio"
  }
]
`
7. Start the VM → first boot fails.
8. Recreate/patch the VM to boot with SATA ("value": "sata") and start → first boot succeeds.
9. After the VM has booted successfully once on SATA, patch the disk bus to virtio or scsi and restart → boots successfully.


**Additional context:**

This looks like Windows may not consider the virtio/scsi storage driver “boot critical” until after a successful first boot / driver initialization phase. Guidance requested on whether this is expected and whether CDI/v2v should recommend or automate “first boot on SATA, then switch bus”.

**Environment:**

CDI version: v1.64.0 (cdi-controller image quay.io/kubevirt/cdi-controller:v1.64.0)

KubeVirt version: v1.6.2

Kubernetes version: v1.33.5 (cluster); kubectl client v1.27.4

Migration method: VMware vCenter → CDI/v2v import using DataVolumeTemplates

Hardware: Bare metal Kubernetes cluster

virtio driver:  virtio-win-0.1.285

OS: Windows Server 2019/2016



", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @person-a141d187! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a known issue with Windows VMs migrated from VMware: even if virtio drivers are installed in the guest before migration, Windows may not treat them as "boot critical" until after a successful boot in the new environment. As a result, the VM fails to boot from a virtio or scsi disk bus on first boot, but works after booting once with SATA and then switching to virtio/scsi. This is due to how Windows handles driver initialization and boot device criticality after hardware changes or migration—Windows often only marks a storage driver as boot critical after it detects and initializes it during a successful boot, which typically happens with a more universally supported bus like SATA. Once this happens, you can safely switch to virtio/scsi and benefit from better performance [reference](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/user_workloads/windows_virtio_drivers/).

There is currently no official KubeVirt or CDI/v2v documentation or automation that handles or recommends this "first boot on SATA, then switch" workflow—it's a community workaround, not an encoded or documented best practice in the project [reference](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/10886). Manual intervention is required for now.

Best practice: after migration, boot the Windows VM with the disk bus set to SATA for the first boot, then patch the disk bus to virtio or scsi and reboot. This ensures Windows initializes the correct drivers as boot critical. If you want to automate this, you'll need to script it in your own migration workflow.

If you want to avoid this manual step in the future, consider using sysprep or unattend.xml to force Windows to pre-load and mark the virtio/scsi drivers as boot critical before migration, but this can be complex and is not always reliable.

Let me know if you want more details on scripting this process or on Windows driver handling in this context.

This is not just a matter of comfort but is actually a (very) big deal.
If virt-api throttles it can cause KubeVirt to hang, which might lead to timeouts, crashes, blocked upgrades and other severe problems. In KubeVirt's case this is especially relevant since we know we have severe scaling problems w.r.t. virt-api, as I reported 4 years ago (!) on https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/7101. I think that the fact that nothing was done at this time proves my point - this is not an easy problem to solve.

My general opinion is that CEL based validations are the future. They become the standard for many Kubernetes facilities (e.g. DRA, CRDs, etc) and for a good reason - they are performed server-side which carries huge benefits - reliability, performance optimizations, but most importantly reducing the need to manage, deploy and auto-scale the validating pods (virt-api in Kubevirt's case).

-----

I suggest the following policy:
* <ins>OpenAPI schema constraints</ins>: Should be used for illegal single-field values that will probably stay illegal forever. For example: an empty name or a negative port number.
* <ins>CEL-based VAPs</ins>: Should be used for validations that do not fit the previous definition, i.e. multi-field validations (e.g. if field X is higher than 5, field Y cannot be empty), validations too complex for OpenAPI schema (e.g. if X's length is higher than 5 do one validation, else do a different validation) and conditions that might change in the future (e.g. field X cannot be populated if the VM is not migratable).
* <ins>Validating webhooks</ins>: These should be discouraged and only be used in rare cases where VAPs are not powerful enough, e.g. a different object (KubeVirt CR for example) needs to be inspected.

----

  name: deny-cool-pod-pods

  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
    - expression: "!object.metadata.name.startsWith('cool-pod')"
      message: "Pods with the 'cool-pod' name prefix are not allowed."
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: deny-cool-pod-pods-binding
spec:
  policyName: deny-cool-pod-pods
  validationActions:
    - Deny

validatingadmissionpolicy.admissionregistration.k8s.io/deny-cool-pod-pods created
validatingadmissionpolicybinding.admissionregistration.k8s.io/deny-cool-pod-pods-binding created

The pods "cool-pod-123" is invalid: : ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'deny-cool-pod-pods' with binding 'deny-cool-pod-pods-binding' denied request: Pods with the 'cool-pod' name prefix are not allowed.

- Allows the cluster admin to remove or modify a validation policy.

As opposed to VAPs, schema-level validations are static, hard to read, modify, update, etc.

-------

I tend to think that in general, VAPs are the go-to way of performing validations.

### Where there seems to be agreement

1. **VAPs (CEL) for complex, cross-field validations** — @person-a2c0ed82, @person-1118c074, @person-f36cb5b0, and others agree that ValidatingAdmissionPolicies are the right tool for validations involving multiple fields, conditional logic, or architectural constraints.

2. **Webhooks remain necessary for external-state validations** — Checks that require cluster state lookups (e.g., verifying a network attachment definition exists) can't be expressed in CEL or OpenAPI and must stay as webhooks.

3. **Organization matters** — @person-1118c074's suggestion of "one VAP per admitter" and @person-05387dcb's concern about VAP sprawl both point to the need for a clear organizational strategy from the start.

### The open question: OpenAPI schema validation

This is where the discussion diverges:

- @person-e665cd28 makes a strong case for OpenAPI — it enables client-side `--dry-run=client` validation, which is a real usability win and not achievable with VAPs alone.
- @person-a2c0ed82 questions whether the OpenAPI tier adds enough value given the maintenance overhead, and whether enum/pattern validations could live in VAPs instead.
- @person-1118c074 suggests a practical split: simple single-field numerics (min/max) and enums in OpenAPI, pattern-based and cross-field in VAPs.

### Proposed three-tier classification

Based on this discussion, I'd propose the following classification for migrating existing webhook validations:

| Tier | Tool | Scope | Example |
|------|------|-------|---------|
| **Static invariants** | OpenAPI (kubebuilder markers) | Single-field type constraints, enums, ranges | `enum: [q35, pc-i440fx]`, `minimum: 1` |
| **Cross-field / arch-dependent** | VAPs (CEL) | Multi-field, conditional, pattern-based | "If CPU model is host-passthrough, then feature policy must be…" |
| **External state** | Webhooks (Go) | Cluster lookups, live resource checks | Verifying referenced ConfigMaps/Secrets exist |

This aligns with @person-1118c074's split and preserves the `--dry-run=client` benefit @person-e665cd28 raised, while keeping OpenAPI usage minimal and low-maintenance.

### On the multi-arch challenge

@person-1c8cf47b correctly identified multi-arch and multi-hypervisor support as the hardest part. One approach: VAP parameter resources (`ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding.paramRef`) that hold per-arch valid values, so a single VAP definition can serve multiple architectures without duplication.

### Next steps

1. Start with a small proof-of-concept migration (e.g., one well-scoped admitter) to validate the approach in practice?
2. Schedule a follow-up call as @person-05387dcb suggested to align on the classification criteria?

I'm actively working on this as part of my GSoC proposal and happy to contribute the initial PoC if the community agrees on a starting point.

**What happened**:

Migrating VMs with long names and backend storage will not work.

The VM migration is in the pending state with the controller spamming the following error:
```
no backend-storage PVC found in VMI volume status
```

The error comes from this function when it tries to retrieve the backend PVC from the VMI:
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/d6b96018473fd5ee559b4f17a244dbd04af4b0fc/pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go#L1401

The name of the VMI being too long, the backend PVC inherits a name that is longer than 63 chars (which is illegal per Kubernetes). The "generateName" key in the `.metadata` detects that and truncates the name.

When the code tries to check if the VMI has the PVC, it doesn't truncate the name. The check will always fail and Kubevirt assumes the PVC is not present on the VMI, eventhough it is, though with a slighly mangled name.

The problem could be mitigated by simply looking up the label on the persistent-state PVC:
```
persistent-state-for=myveryveryveryverylongvmnamethatwilldefinitelynotwork
```

The value of this key should always be 63 char maximum as the initial VM/VMI can't have a name longer than that.

To make the change backward compatible and avoid unnecessary lookups, if the first check fails, we can fallback to the second one.

**What you expected to happen**:

The VM gets successfuly migrated.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

- Create a VM with persistent EFI/TPM and a 63 char name
- Witness the `persistent-state-for-` name PVC being mangled
- Migrate the VM
- Witness the VMIMigration stuck in the "Pending" state

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): 1.7.0
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.34.1

The missing amd64 images in the nightly builds are caused by a gap in the manifest publishing logic: the multi-arch manifest (which includes amd64) is only created and pushed from the s390x job. If the s390x job fails or doesn't run, the amd64 images are built and pushed, but the manifest list isn't published, so the registry lacks the amd64 variant in the image index. This leads to ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff errors for pods trying to pull amd64 images, as seen in your logs [source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirtci/pull/1613).

The image upload failure with "Healthcheck requested" and a 200 OK status from quay.io is not standard. The publish.sh script uses podman and skopeo for pushing images and manifests, but doesn't have custom error handling for this registry response—any error simply bubbles up through the shell's `set -e` behavior and podman/skopeo output [source](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirtci/blob/034a027d27924779be25a50e6e6f4fcf61bc0543/publish.sh#L5-L250). This suggests a registry-side issue or a miscommunication between the client and quay.io, possibly related to recent changes in container runtime or registry API behavior.

To resolve this, ensure the s390x job always runs and completes successfully, so the manifest list is published and includes amd64. If you need amd64-only manifests, consider updating publish.sh to publish the manifest from the amd64 job as well. Improving error handling for unexpected registry responses in publish.sh could also help catch silent failures earlier.

3. **Add unit tests** covering: valid model accepted, invalid model rejected, special modes accepted, empty string accepted.

> Should an unrecognized CPU model result in a **hard rejection** or an **admission warning**?
