### 1. "At least one node" vs "all nodes" - why this approach?

You're absolutely right that the **primary and most common use case** for `spec.configuration.cpuModel` is to find a CPU model that's common to all cluster nodes. Setting a default that only works on a subset of nodes would indeed be problematic for most deployments.

However, I chose "at least one node" validation instead of "all nodes" to avoid breaking a valid (though less common) edge case: **intentionally heterogeneous clusters**.

For example, consider a cluster with:
- 10 nodes with Intel Haswell CPUs (older generation)
- 5 nodes with newer Intel Cascadelake-Server CPUs

In this setup, if we required the `cpuModel` to exist on **all** nodes, you wouldn't be able to set any default at all the intersection would be empty. With "at least one node" validation, you can set `cpuModel: "Haswell"` knowing that new VMIs (without explicit CPU overrides) will schedule to the 10 Haswell nodes. The 5 newer Cascadelake nodes remain available for VMIs that explicitly request `Cascadelake-Server` to take advantage of newer CPU features.

That said, I completely agree that this is the **edge case**, not the common case, and users attempting the common case deserve clear feedback.

### 2. Warning when the model isn't common to all nodes

**Absolutely agree - this is a great suggestion!** I'll add an admission warning when the specified CPU model is only supported by a subset of nodes. Something like:

Warning: cpuModel "Haswell" is only supported by 10 of 15 cluster nodes. New VMIs using this cluster-wide default will only be schedulable on 67% of cluster nodes. For cluster-wide VM scheduling, choose a CPU model that is common to all nodes.


This way:
- Users pursuing the common use case (cluster-wide default) get immediate, clear feedback that they haven't achieved it
- The warning explains the impact (percentage of nodes where scheduling will work)
- It guides users toward the solution (pick a model common to all nodes)
- But it doesn't break the heterogeneous cluster edge case for users who intentionally need it

### 3. What happens after node maintenance removes nodes with that CPU model?

**This is a really important catch - thank you for raising it!** You've identified a genuine bug in the current implementation.

Right now, `validateCPUModel` runs on **every** KubeVirt CR update, regardless of whether `cpuModel` is being changed. This creates a problematic scenario:

1. Day 1: You set `cpuModel: "Haswell"` (validates successfully )
2. Day 30: All Haswell nodes are removed during planned maintenance
3. Day 31: You try to update a completely unrelated KubeVirt setting (e.g., enable a new feature gate or update TLS configuration)
4. **The update gets blocked ** because the validation re-runs and `cpuModel: "Haswell"` no longer matches any nodes, even though you're not modifying the CPU model at all

This is clearly not the right behavior - it would prevent necessary configuration updates.

**The fix:** Only validate `cpuModel` when it's actually being changed. This follows the exact same pattern already used in this file for other configuration fields like `SeccompConfiguration`:

```go
}
```

- Subsequent unrelated KubeVirt CR updates aren't blocked if node topology changes over time
- If you do try to change [cpuModel](vscode-file://vscode-app/usr/share/code/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) to a new value after maintenance removes nodes, you'll get appropriate validation feedback for the new value
- Existing VMIs with their own explicit CPU model settings continue to work (this is a cluster-wide default, not a constraint on running VMs)

This sounds like a known race condition issue during KubeVirt upgrades that can cause ServiceMonitor and PrometheusRule resources to be disabled ([#16593](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16593)).

When the install-strategy job regenerates the ConfigMap during upgrade, it only includes monitoring resources if it can find the monitoring ServiceAccount at that exact moment. If the ServiceAccount isn't present due to timing issues, the ConfigMap is created without ServiceMonitor, and VM metrics stop being scraped.

**To verify this is the issue:**
```bash
kubectl get servicemonitor -n kubevirt
kubectl get prometheusrule -n kubevirt
```

**Workaround:** Explicitly set `serviceMonitorNamespace` in your KubeVirt CR configuration:
```yaml
spec:
  configuration:
    serviceMonitorNamespace: kubevirt
```

This has been [confirmed to resolve the issue](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/13829#issuecomment-2631211923) for affected users.

You can also check if the base metric `kubevirt_vmi_info` is being collected in Prometheus—if it returns data but `kubevirt_vmi_phase_count` doesn't, the recording rule isn't being evaluated (which would confirm the PrometheusRule is missing).

**2. Check if the metrics service exists:**

**3. Test if virt-controller is actually exposing metrics** (this rules out Prometheus scraping issues):
```bash

```

If the ServiceMonitor is missing but port-forward shows the metrics, the workaround is to add `serviceMonitorNamespace: kubevirt` to your KubeVirt CR:
```yaml
spec:
  configuration:
    serviceMonitorNamespace: kubevirt
```

This should trigger virt-operator to regenerate the install strategy ConfigMap and include the ServiceMonitor.

**Solution**: Upgrade to the latest v1.6.x patch release that includes the fix from PR #16219.

**Workaround** (until you can upgrade): Space out hotplug operations to at least 10+ seconds between changes to avoid triggering the race condition.

**What happened**:
I have VMs that have RWX root storage and RWO volumes that are hotplugged (using the DeclarativeHotplugVolumes feature). The hotplugged RWO storage is local disk using TopoLVM and therefore the PVs have a strict node affinity.

When I restart a VM with this configuration, the scheduler doesn't take into consideration the node affinity of the hotplugged storage as technically, on the VM pod the only volumeMount is of the RWX root volume. Due to this, the VM pod may start on any node.

When the VM pod starts up, the hotplug helper pod is scheduled on the same node as the VM pod, but it gets stuck in Pending since the VM was scheduled onto a node that wasn't local to the hotplugged storage and the hotplug helper pod is trying to mount a volume that resides on another node.

If a VMI has hotplugged storage and that storage is Bound, it should be scheduled with an affinity for the node where the hotplugged storage actually resides.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Create a VM with portable RWX root storage
2. Hotplug a non-portable RWO volume to the VM
3. Restart the VM and watch as it's scheduled to a node which is not local to the hotplugged storage

**Additional context**:
I'm using DataVolumes from CDI for all my volumes and the root disk imports a disk image while the RWO local storage uses 'blank" as the source.

This is indeed a known architectural limitation in KubeVirt. The root cause is that **hotplugged volumes are not included in the VM pod spec**, so the Kubernetes scheduler has no visibility into their node affinity constraints when placing the VM. Attachment pods are then created with [hard node affinity to the VM's node](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/services/template.go#L1007-L1023), creating the circular dependency you're hitting.

I didn't find an existing issue tracking this specific scenario, so this appears to be a new bug report. There are related issues around [storage topology awareness during VM scheduling](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14239#issuecomment-2723809838) that highlight this as a broader architectural gap.

**Workaround**: The most practical approach is to manually pin your VM to the node where the RWO storage resides using node affinity:

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
                operator: In
                values: [node-with-your-rwo-volume]
```

This loses scheduling flexibility but ensures the VM lands on the correct node. Alternatively, if your storage backend supports it, using RWX storage for the hotplugged volumes would avoid the constraint entirely.

## Description

 The admitHotplugCPU function in the VMI update admission webhook dereferences oldCPUTopology.MaxSockets   
  and newCPUTopology.MaxSockets without first checking whether the pointers are nil.

  Spec.Domain.CPU is an optional field — any VMI that does not explicitly define a CPU topology will have
  nil here. When such a VMI is updated, the admission webhook panics, causing the request to fail with an
  internal server error instead of a proper validation response.



**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

  1. Create a VMI with no spec.domain.cpu field set
  2. Perform any kubectl patch or update on that VMI
  3. The virt-api admission webhook panics

 **Expected Behaviour**

  VMI updates where spec.domain.cpu is nil should be admitted without error. There is no maxSockets
  constraint to enforce if no CPU topology is defined.

  **Actual Behaviour**

  Panic / nil pointer dereference in virt-api, resulting in a 500 Internal Server Error for the update
  request.

Looking at the code, the [`admitHotplugCPU` function](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-api/webhooks/validating-webhook/admitters/vmi-update-admitter.go#L194-L206) directly dereferences `oldCPUTopology.MaxSockets` and `newCPUTopology.MaxSockets` at [line 196](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-api/webhooks/validating-webhook/admitters/vmi-update-admitter.go#L196) without any nil checks.

Interestingly, the [`admitHotplugMemory` function](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-api/webhooks/validating-webhook/admitters/vmi-update-admitter.go#L208-L214) directly below it in the same file **does include proper nil checks**:

```go
if oldMemory == nil ||
    oldMemory.MaxGuest == nil ||
    newMemory == nil ||
    newMemory.MaxGuest == nil {
    return nil
}
```

The fix would follow the same pattern:

```go
func admitHotplugCPU(oldCPUTopology, newCPUTopology *v1.CPU) *admissionv1.AdmissionResponse {
    if oldCPUTopology == nil || newCPUTopology == nil {
        return nil
    }
    // existing validation logic...
}
```

There are related nil pointer issues being addressed in the project — [PR #16665](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16665) recently fixed a similar issue for guest memory, and [#16395](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16395) tracks another CPU-related nil pointer bug on ARM64.

{"author": "person-c80cee2c", "body": "### Description

GenerateDomainForTargetCPUSetAndTopology in pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/cpudedicated/cpudedicated.go directly accesses vmi.Status.MigrationState.TargetCPUSet and vmi.Status.MigrationState.TargetNodeTopology as its first operations, with no nil guard on MigrationState.

MigrationState is only set during an active live migration. The function is called from live-migration-source.go and cpu_hook.go. Any ordering issue, unexpected call, or race condition where the state has not yet been populated will cause an immediate nil pointer dereference that crashes virt-launcher.

  The package has no tests at all, so there is no regression coverage for this
  function.

  Root Cause

```go
  func GenerateDomainForTargetCPUSetAndTopology(vmi *v1.VirtualMachineInstance,
  domSpec *api.DomainSpec) (*api.Domain, error) {
      var targetTopology cmdv1.Topology
      targetNodeCPUSet := vmi.Status.MigrationState.TargetCPUSet          // panics
   if MigrationState is nil
      err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(vmi.Status.MigrationState.TargetNodeTopology),
  &targetTopology) // same
```

**What happened**:
  virt-launcher panics, the pod is killed, and the running VM is lost.

**What you expected to happen**:
  The function should return a descriptive error when MigrationState is nil,
  allowing the caller to handle the situation gracefully instead of crashing.

Thanks for the detailed bug report. This is consistent with similar nil pointer dereference issues that have been found and fixed in related CPU topology code:
- [Issue #16395](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16395) - panic in `AdjustDomainForTopologyAndCPUSet()` fixed in [PR #16396](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16396)
- [Issue #16271](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16271) - panic with `ioThreads` and `dedicatedCpuPlacement` enabled

The codebase already has an established pattern for guarding against nil `MigrationState` used in 30+ other files:

```go
if vmi.Status.MigrationState == nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("MigrationState is nil")
}
```

A fix would involve adding this nil check at the start of the function and returning a descriptive error, consistent with the patterns used elsewhere.

  "selector is immutable" rejection

  **Affected File:**
  pkg/virt-api/webhooks/validating-webhook/admitters/vmpool-admitter.go:182-196

  After json.Unmarshal(ar.Request.OldObject.Raw, oldPool) fails, the code appends
  an UnexpectedServerResponse cause but does not return. It falls through to
  DeepEqual(pool.Spec.Selector, oldPool.Spec.Selector) where oldPool is a
  zero-value struct. Since pool.Spec.Selector is never equal to a zero-value
  selector, every pool update that triggers an unmarshal error (corrupted
  OldObject) also produces a spurious "selector is immutable" rejection on top of
  the real error.

  **Suggested Fix:** return causes immediately after appending the unmarshal cause.

  ---
  ### Bug 2 

— netstat: ReadPodInterfaceCache error silently swallowed with //FIXME

  **Affected File:** pkg/network/setup/netstat.go:240-243

```go

      //FIXME error handling?
      podInterface = data
  }
```

  When the pod interface cache file is missing or corrupt, the error is completely
  ignored. An empty PodIfaceCacheData{} is used without any log message. This makes
   debugging VMI network status issues (missing IPs, etc.) extremely difficult.

  **Suggested Fix:** Log the error at V(4) and continue — preserving the non-breaking behavior
  while making failures observable.

  ---
  ### Bug 3

 — replicaset: only the first error returned from concurrent scale operations

  **Affected File:** pkg/virt-controller/watch/replicaset/replicaset.go:321-330 and 796-804

{"author": "person-c80cee2c", "body": "Three independent bugs found across the migration proxy, network link naming, and hotplug disk path subsystems.

  ### Bug 1 — `conn` never closed in `migration-proxy.handleConnection`

  **File:** `pkg/virt-handler/migration-proxy/migration-proxy.go`

  - After a successful outbound dial, `fd` (inbound) is closed via `defer fd.Close()` but the outbound `conn`
  has no corresponding `defer conn.Close()`. When `stopChan` is signalled, the goroutines exit but `conn` is
   never closed, leaking a file descriptor for every migration connection. Over many live migrations this
  causes file descriptor exhaustion in virt-handler.

  ### Bug 2 — `GenerateNewBridgedVmiInterfaceName` produces names exceeding IFNAMSIZ

  **File:** `pkg/network/link/names.go`

  - The function appends `-nic` to the trimmed interface name but never validates that the result fits within
  the 15-character Linux `IFNAMSIZ - 1` limit. On interfaces whose trimmed name is already 12+ characters,
  the generated name silently exceeds the kernel limit, causing mismatches and potentially incorrect routing
   for bridged VMI interfaces.

  ### Bug 3 — `GetFileSystemDiskTargetPathFromHostView` returns non-nil path on error

  **File:** `pkg/hotplug-disk/hotplug-disk.go`

  - On the early error path at line 97, the function returns `targetPath, err` — a potentially non-nil
  `*safepath.Path` alongside a non-nil error. The sibling return on line 101 correctly returns `nil, err`.
  Callers that assume path is always nil on error risk a nil dereference or use of an invalid path.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

  - Bug 1: Run many successive live migrations and we can observe fd count on virt-handler pod growing without
  bound.
  - Bug 2: Create a VMI with a pod interface whose trimmed name is ≥ 12 characters, we can observe bridge NIC name
  - Bug 3: Call `GetFileSystemDiskTargetPathFromHostView` with an invalid UID and inspect the returned path
  value.

### Expected Behavior

  - Outbound migration connection is closed when the proxy stops.
  - `GenerateNewBridgedVmiInterfaceName` returns an error for names that would exceed 15 characters.
  - `GetFileSystemDiskTargetPathFromHostView` returns `nil, err` consistently on all error paths.

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
I verified all three bugs through code examination:

**Bug 1 — Connection leak in `handleConnection`** ✅ Confirmed

The [handleConnection function](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-handler/migration-proxy/migration-proxy.go#L439-L490) closes the inbound `fd` with `defer fd.Close()` (line 440), but the outbound `conn` from `tls.Dial()` or `net.Dial()` (lines 448-458) has no corresponding `defer conn.Close()`. When `stopChan` triggers (line 487), the function exits without closing `conn`.

**Fix:** Add `defer conn.Close()` after successful dial around line 463.

**Bug 2 — IFNAMSIZ violation** ⚠️ Partially Confirmed

The [GenerateNewBridgedVmiInterfaceName function](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/network/link/names.go#L47-L50) has no built-in length validation. However, validation is delegated upstream—the [namescheme package sets maxIfaceNameLen to 11](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/network/namescheme/networknamescheme.go#L40) (accounting for `-nic` suffix), so current usage patterns via namescheme are safe. The function itself remains vulnerable if called with unconstrained inputs.

**Fix:** Add defensive length validation within the function.

**Bug 3 — Non-nil path on error** ✅ Confirmed

At [line 97 of hotplug-disk.go](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/hotplug-disk/hotplug-disk.go#L97), the function returns `targetPath, err` instead of `nil, err`. The sibling return at line 101 correctly uses `nil, err`, and the similar function `GetFileSystemDirectoryTargetPathFromHostView` at [line 80](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/hotplug-disk/hotplug-disk.go#L80) also correctly returns `nil, err`.

**Fix:** Change line 97 to `return nil, err`.

**What happened**:
`WorkloadUpdateController.sync()` in `pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go` spawns one  goroutine per VMI in `data.abortChangeVMIs`. Inside each goroutine the code does a bare `=` assignment to `err`, a variable that was declared in the outer function scope at line 464:

  ```go
  key, err := controller.KeyFunc(kv)   // line 464 — outer err
  ...
  for _, vmi := range data.abortChangeVMIs {
      go func(vmi *virtv1.VirtualMachineInstance) {
          for _, mig := range migList {
              err = c.clientset...Delete(...)   // captures outer err — DATA RACE
```

  When data.abortChangeVMIs contains more than one VMI, multiple goroutines run concurrently and all write to the same err variable without any synchronisation. go test -race flags this immediately.

--- 
  
Second issue — potential deadlock on errChan

  errChan is allocated with capacity wgLen, where wgLen counts exactly one slot per abortChangeVMI goroutine. But each goroutine loops over migList and can send multiple errors (one per migration deletion failure). If a single VMI has ≥ 2 pending migrations and both deletions fail, the goroutine blocks on the second errChan <- err (channel full), wg.Done() is never called, and wg.Wait() deadlocks forever.


**What you expected to happen**:

 - Each goroutine uses its own local err variable.
 - At most one error is sent to errChan per goroutine, keeping the channel
  from overflowing.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

- Race: create a KubeVirt upgrade with two or more VMIs that have the WorkloadUpdateMigrationAbortionAnnotation set and active workload-update migrations. Run go test -race ./pkg/virt-controller/... — race reported.
 - Deadlock: have a single VMI with two active workload-update migrations both of which fail to delete. virt-controller goroutine hangs indefinitely.

Thanks for filing this issue! I can confirm both bugs you've described are real and exist in the code.

**Bug #1 - Data Race**: You're correct. The [abort migration goroutines (lines 636-654)](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L636-L654) use `err = ...` (assignment) instead of `err := ...` (declaration), which captures the [outer-scoped `err` from line 464](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L464). Multiple goroutines read/write to this shared variable concurrently without synchronization. Notably, the [migration](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L559-L601) and [eviction](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L605-L633) goroutines in the same function correctly use local declarations.

**Bug #2 - Channel Issues**: The errChan buffer is [sized to `wgLen`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L552-L555) (one per goroutine), but abort goroutines can send multiple errors when looping over `migList`. Additionally, the [error handling logic](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L655-L663) only reads **one** error from the channel, silently discarding the rest.

**Related Work**: These are the **exact same patterns** that were recently identified and fixed in other KubeVirt components:
- [PR #16974](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16974) fixed silent error loss in `replicaset.go` using the same single-error-read pattern
- [Issue #16973](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16973) documents three error-handling deficiencies including this pattern
- [PR #16961](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16961) fixed channel-related panics in profiler handlers

This suggests workload-updater.go should be addressed as part of the ongoing concurrency safety effort across the codebase.

While going through the code I noticed something that looks wrong regardless of this specific regression: ConsoleRequestHandler uses NewRawStreamer which has keepAliveClient: nil, meaning no WebSocket pings are ever sent on the console connection. Compare that to portforward which uses NewWebsocketStreamer with keepAliveClientStream — pinging every second with a 60s read deadline — and doesn't have this problem. Console was simply never given the same treatment. This gap also looks related to #6493.
That said, I want to be honest — the timing doesn't cleanly fit a keepalive expiry. The disconnect happens at exactly T=39s, which is precisely when the workload finishes, not at any fixed timeout boundary. So the trigger seems to be the transition from active data flow to idle, rather than a timer running out. My suspicion is that something in the k8s 1.34 network path behaves differently for idle streaming connections, and the raw io.Copy via UnderlyingConn() isn't equipped to handle it — but I can't confirm this without a live environment to add debug logging to Handle() in streamer.go.
The approach I'm thinking of: Add keepAliveClient: keepAliveClientStream to the console streamer — same pattern already used by portforward, no new code needed. It's the right fix for the keepalive gap regardless of what exactly triggers the disconnect. But I want to flag that it may not be the complete story.

Before opening a PR, I'd love to understand if anything changed in the k8s 1.34 aggregation layer around idle streaming connections — that would close the last open question. Also if anyone can reproduce this with a quick log on which goroutine in Handle() returns first and what error it carries, that would really help confirm the trigger.

during high volume serial output, the TCP transmit buffer becomes congested, causing the websocket's WriteMessage to block for extended periods while holding the connection's write mutex `c.mu`. when the kube-apiserver proxy sends a keep alive `Ping`, the default PingHandler tries to reply but fails quickly due to the mutex contention, dropping the Pong. repeatedly dropped Pongs cause - terminate the connection with 1006.

```go
clientSocket.SetPingHandler(func(message string) error {
	err := clientSocket.WriteControl(websocket.PongMessage, []byte(message), time.Now().Add(10*time.Second))
	if err == websocket.ErrCloseSent {
		return nil
	} else if e, ok := err.(net.Error); ok && e.Timeout() {
		return nil
	}
	return err
})
```

**What happened**:
`WorkloadUpdateController.sync()` in  `pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go` launches one goroutine per VMI in `evictionCandidates`. Inside the goroutine, `CurrentVMIPod` is called to find the launcher pod:

  ```go
  pod, err := controller.CurrentVMIPod(vmi, c.podIndexer)
  if err != nil {
      ...
      errChan <- err
      // ← NO return
  }
  // pod may be nil here in two different ways ↓
  err = c.clientset.CoreV1().Pods(...).EvictV1beta1(ctx,
      &policy.Eviction{
          ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{
              Name: pod.Name,      // PANIC
```

  CurrentVMIPod has two nil-pod return paths:

  Path A — (nil, err): podIndexer.ByIndex fails. The goroutine logs the error and sends it to errChan, but then falls through to  pod.Name because there is no return. Panics virt-controller.

  Path B — (nil, nil): No pod is found in the informer cache (e.g. during a KubeVirt operator upgrade when pods are briefly absent from the   cache). The err != nil guard is never entered, and the code falls directly to pod.Name. Guaranteed panic — no error branch at all.

  Path B is particularly dangerous: it is a normal transient state during every KubeVirt upgrade, so virt-controller will crash-loop until the pod reappears in the informer cache.

**What you expected to happen**:
  - Path A: goroutine sends the error to errChan and returns; pod is never dereferenced.
  - Path B: goroutine logs a warning and returns; the controller  re-queues naturally and retries on the next sync cycle.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
  - Trigger a KubeVirt operator upgrade with VMIs that are candidates for  eviction (WorkloadUpdateMethodEvict enabled, non-migratable outdated  VMIs). During reconciliation, the launcher pod briefly disappears from the informer cache → CurrentVMIPod returns (nil, nil) → panic.

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report! I can confirm this is a valid bug that has existed since the [original implementation in January 2021](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/commit/f3f7819206fb152946a5239aea3c6021e3efc21f).

Looking at the [eviction goroutine code (lines 604-634)](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/virt-controller/watch/workload-updater/workload-updater.go#L604-L634), your analysis is correct:

- **Path A**: The error is logged and sent to `errChan`, but execution continues without a `return`, leading to nil dereference
- **Path B**: [`CurrentVMIPod` intentionally returns `(nil, nil)`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/bc43cc3c040b9eca1afd10b7abc776b1779ddfd9/pkg/controller/controller.go#L323-L359) when no matching pod is found (line 358), which bypasses the error check entirely

This bug is **not yet fixed**. While several nil pointer fixes have been merged recently for related components ([PR #15008](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15008), [PR #16788](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16788)), none address this specific issue. There's also an [open PR #16980](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16980) fixing data race and deadlock issues in the *abort migration* goroutines of the same `sync()` method, but it doesn't cover the eviction goroutine.

Your suggested fix aligns with patterns used in those merged PRs - adding a `return` after sending to `errChan` and a nil check for `pod` before dereferencing.

This looks like a **known critical bug in KubeVirt v1.7.0** (see [issue #16271](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16271)). The bug involves an order-of-operations problem where CPU pinning operations attempt to access uninitialized IOThreads structures, causing virt-launcher panics during VM initialization.

**The fix ([PR #16327](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16327)) was merged on December 15, 2025** — after v1.7.0 was released (November 22, 2025). This means v1.7.0 does not include the fix.

**Workarounds for now:**
1. **Temporarily disable `isolateEmulatorThread`** until you can upgrade (as you've discovered works)
2. **Wait for v1.8.0** or build from the main branch which includes the fix

**Additional requirements you may need (for when the bug is fixed):**
- Since you're on K3s bare-metal, ensure the Kubernetes CPU Manager has `static` policy enabled via kubelet configuration
- If your nodes have SMT/hyperthreading enabled with `full-pcpus-only` policy, you'll also need:
  - Enable the `AlignCPUs` feature gate in the KubeVirt CR
  - Add the `alpha.kubevirt.io/EmulatorThreadCompleteToEvenParity: "true"` annotation to your VM

Could you share the virt-launcher pod logs? That would help confirm this is the same bug. Also, are you explicitly using IOThreads in your configuration?

It looks like [PR #16327](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16327) (the fix for the original [#16271](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16271)) was merged to the main branch on December 15, 2025 but was **never cherry-picked to the release-1.8 branch**, so it's not included in v1.8.0 or v1.8.1.

On top of that, there's a **second related bug** tracked in [#17247](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/17247) — a slice bounds panic in the IOThread CPU pinning code when `dedicatedCpuPlacement` is enabled. That one was confirmed to reproduce on v1.7.0, v1.7.2, and v1.8.0-rc.0, and its proposed fix ([PR #16996](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16996)) is still open and unmerged.

So there are two unfixed issues in v1.8.1 affecting this code path. For now, disabling `isolateEmulatorThread` (and if applicable, removing any `ioThreadsPolicy`) remains the workaround.

It might be worth raising the backporting question with the maintainers — PR #16327 at minimum seems like a candidate for a v1.8.x patch release.

**What happened**:
In `pkg/virt-launcher/standalone/standalone.go`, `HandleStandaloneMode`                                                                                 
  tries to unmarshal the `STANDALONE_VMI` env var as YAML first, then falls                                                                               
  back to JSON. If both fail, the code logs and panics using the **YAML                                                                                   
  error** (`err`), not the JSON error (`jsonErr`).                 

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
  1. Set `STANDALONE_VMI` to an invalid string (not valid YAML or JSON).                                                                                  
  2. Launch virt-launcher in standalone mode.
  3. Observe the panic message — it reports the YAML parse error, completely                                                                              
     hiding the JSON parse error. 

### Root Cause                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                          
  ```go                                                     
  // standalone.go:38-43
  if err := yaml.Unmarshal(...); err != nil {                                                                                                             
      if jsonErr := json.Unmarshal(...); jsonErr != nil {                                                                                                 
          log.Log.Reason(err).Error(...)  // ← YAML err, not jsonErr                                                                                      
          panic(err)                      // ← YAML err, not jsonErr                                                                                      
      }                                                                                                                                                   
  }                                                                                                                                                       
   ```                                                                                                                                                        
  jsonErr is declared but err (the YAML error) is what gets surfaced.                                                                                     
  
  ### Impact                                                                                                                                                  
                                                            
  Operators debugging a misconfigured STANDALONE_VMI value see a                                                                                          
  misleading error message, making diagnosis unnecessarily difficult.
                                                                                                                                                          
  ### Fix                                                       
                                                                                                                                                          
  Replace both err references inside the JSON fallback branch with

**What happened**:
`handleConnection` in `pkg/virt-handler/migration-proxy/migration-proxy.go` closes the inbound connection (`fd`) via `defer fd.Close()` but never closes the outbound connection (`conn`) after a successful dial. When `stopChan` is signalled (e.g. migration ends or virt-handler stops), the goroutine exits without closing `conn`, leaking the underlying file descriptor.                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                
  ### Root Cause                                                                                                
                                                                                                              
  ```go
  func (m *migrationProxy) handleConnection(fd net.Conn) {
      defer fd.Close()                                                                                                                                                                    
      conn, err = tls.Dial(...)                                                                   
      if err != nil {                                                                                           
          return                                                                                              
      }                                                                                                         
      select {                                                                                                  
      case <-m.stopChan:                                                                                      
          return  
      }                                                                                                         
  }
```
                                                                                                                
  ### Impact                                                                                                      

  Every live migration that goes through this proxy leaks one outbound TCP or TLS connection file descriptor in virt-handler. In environments with frequent or large-scale live migrations this causes file descriptor exhaustion, ultimately making virt-handler unable to open new connections or files and crashing the node agent.                                                                         
                                                                                                                
  ### Fix

{"author": "person-c80cee2c", "body": "
**What happened**:

  ### Summary                                               

In `pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go`, `removeHandOffKey`is only called when a migration object disappears from the informer cache. When a migration reaches a final phase (`Succeeded` or `Failed`), the entry is never removed from `handOffMap` — it persists until Kubernetes garbage-collects the object, which can be arbitrarily delayed.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                
  ### Root Cause                                                                                                
  
  ```go                                                                                                                             
  if !exists {                                                                                                  
      c.removeHandOffKey(key)   //  called on object deletion
      return nil                                                                                                
  }                                                                                                                                                                  
  // IsFinal() block — no removeHandOffKey call                                                  
  if migration.IsFinal() {
      c.garbageCollectFinalizedMigrations(vmi)  // may keep object alive                                        
      // removeHandOffKey is NEVER called here                                                                
  }
```
                                                                                                                
  ### Impact                                                                                                        
  
  Memory leak: handOffMap is an unbounded in-memory map[string]struct{}.  In clusters with frequent live migrations, or where TTLSecondsAfterFinished is long / GC is slow, the map grows indefinitely, leaking memory in virt-controller.                                                                                              
                                                                                                                
@person-cb060f8c  @person-f36cb5b0                                                                                        
                                                                                                                ", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
I can confirm this analysis is correct. Looking at the code:

1. **Entry addition**: [`addHandOffKey`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/18f09e6ef8d9f7f55b024f27cd644a2ea21bc23d/pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go#L1286) is called during target pod handoff after the VMI status is patched.

2. **Entry removal**: [`removeHandOffKey`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/18f09e6ef8d9f7f55b024f27cd644a2ea21bc23d/pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go#L381) is only called when `!exists` in the execute method — meaning the migration object was deleted from Kubernetes.

3. **No cleanup on IsFinal()**: The [`IsFinal()` block](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/18f09e6ef8d9f7f55b024f27cd644a2ea21bc23d/pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go#L437-L449) performs garbage collection and finalizer removal, but never calls `removeHandOffKey`.

The fix would be straightforward — add `removeHandOffKey` in the `IsFinal()` block:

```go
if migration.IsFinal() {
    c.removeHandOffKey(controller.MigrationKey(migration))  // Add this line
    
    err = c.garbageCollectFinalizedMigrations(vmi)
    // ...
}
```

Since the [garbage collection buffer is hardcoded to 5 migrations per VMI](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/18f09e6ef8d9f7f55b024f27cd644a2ea21bc23d/pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go#L88-L91), the leak is bounded but still grows linearly with the number of VMIs. For large clusters with frequent migrations, this can add up.

Note: There have been similar memory leak fixes in this area recently — [PR #15642](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15642) (PVC expectation key mismatch) and [PR #15513](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15513) (priority queue management).

{"author": "person-c80cee2c", "body": "**What happened**:

### Summary                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                
 In `pkg/virt-handler/device-manager/socket_device.go`,  `monitorDevice` sets up an `fsnotify` watcher on two directories. The first one correctly watches the device directory. The second one is intended to watch the directory containing the kubelet device-plugin socket (`dpi.socketPath`), but due to a copy-paste bug i guess,                                         it watches `deviceDir` again — a no-op since the path was already added.                                      
                                                                                                                
  The event loop checks `event.Name == dpi.socketPath` to   detect kubelet restarts, but because `filepath.Dir(dpi.socketPath)` is   never added to the watcher, fsnotify never emits events for that path. The kubelet-restart branch is therefore **dead code** — it can never fire.                                                                                                         
                                                            
  ### Root Cause                                                                                                
                                                            
  ```go
  //  correct
  err = watcher.Add(deviceDir)                                                                                  
  
  //BUG: should be filepath.Dir(dpi.socketPath)                                                     
  err = watcher.Add(deviceDir)   // duplicate, wrong path   
                                                                                                                
  //  unreachable: dpi.socketPath's dir is not watched                                                
  } else if event.Name == dpi.socketPath && event.Op == fsnotify.Remove {                                       
      logger.Infof("device socket file for device %s was removed, kubelet probably restarted.")                 
      return nil                                            
  } 
```                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                
 ### Impact                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                
  When kubelet restarts it removes the device plugin socket. The device plugin process never detects the removal and never triggers re-registration with the new kubelet instance. Devices such as  vhost-user NICs and SR-IOV VFs become permanently orphaned — pods  requesting those devices on the affected node silently fail to schedule, and the only recovery is a manual virt-handler restart.

[PR #16073](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16073) addresses this bug as part of a broader device plugin framework refactoring — it corrects the copy-paste bug and also implements fsnotify best practices by watching directories instead of files (since watchers are lost when files are deleted).

{"author": "person-f60a4e97", "body": "**What happened**:  
When downgrading KubeVirt with running VMIs still present, `virt-handler` can fail to reconcile an existing ghost record for a running VMI because the stored socket path and the rediscovered live socket path differ only by path normalization.

In the failing case, the ghost record contains a socket path like:

`/pods/<podUID>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/sockets/launcher-sock`

but the downgraded `virt-handler` rediscovers the live socket as:

`//pods/<podUID>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/sockets/launcher-sock`

These refer to the same location semantically, but `AddGhostRecord()` compares them as raw strings and rejects the record with:

`can not add ghost record when entry already exists with differing socket file location`

After that, the VMI is repeatedly re-enqueued and is not managed normally.

This appears to be caused by a change where newer KubeVirt versions normalize the socket path with `filepath.Clean()`, while older versions do not.

**What you expected to happen**:  
`virt-handler` should not fail ghost record reconciliation just because one path is stored as `/pods/...` and the other is discovered as `//pods/...`.

Even if downgrade with running VMIs is not considered a supported operational scenario, logically equivalent socket paths should be normalized or canonicalized before comparison so that reconciliation does not fail for the same underlying socket location.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:  
1. Start with a KubeVirt version where the socket path helper uses `filepath.Clean()`.
2. Start one or more VMIs and let them remain running.
3. Downgrade KubeVirt to a version where the socket path helper does not use `filepath.Clean()`.
4. Let the downgraded `virt-handler` rediscover the running VMI and its launcher socket.
5. Observe that ghost record reconciliation fails with:  
   `can not add ghost record when entry already exists with differing socket file location`

A successful comparison case can also be seen when both the writing version and the reading version use the same unnormalized `//pods/...` path format. In that case, reconciliation succeeds.

**Additional context**:  
The issue appears to come from inconsistent socket path canonicalization across versions.

Example of the relevant code pattern:

Newer version:
```
func SocketDirectoryOnHost(podUID string) string {
    return filepath.Clean(fmt.Sprintf("/%s/%s/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/sockets", podsBaseDir, podUID))
}

```
Older version:

```
func SocketDirectoryOnHost(podUID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("/%s/%s/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/sockets", podsBaseDir, podUID)
}

```

With podsBaseDir = "/pods", the formatted path becomes "//pods/..." before cleaning.
So one version stores /pods/... while the other later rediscovers //pods/....

The issue is therefore not that the socket location is actually different, but that ghost record reconciliation depends on raw string equality for a path that is not normalized consistently across versions.

It looks like AddGhostRecord() should normalize/canonicalize both paths before comparing them.

Environment:

KubeVirt version (use virtctl version): observed on downgrade from v1.7.0 to v1.5.0

Kubernetes version (use kubectl version): N/A

VM or VMI specifications: VMI was already running before downgrade

Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A

OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): N/A

Kernel (e.g. uname -a): N/A

Install tools: N/A

Others: downgrade from v1.5.0 to v1.1.0 did not reproduce the issue because both versions used the same unnormalized //pods/... path format", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @person-f60a4e97! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed report! Your analysis is correct. This issue stems from [PR #15325](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15325) (merged August 2025), which added `filepath.Clean()` to socket path handling because the safepath library couldn't process double slashes (`//`).

The current code in [`cache.go`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/f7ab74fe8ddb53cb2ed1d0069c3474f28eb5f672/pkg/virt-handler/cache/cache.go#L155-L197) does clean the stored record before comparison:

```go
if ok && filepath.Clean(record.SocketFile) != socketFile {
    return fmt.Errorf("can not add ghost record when entry already exists with differing socket file location")
}
```

However, the problem in your downgrade scenario is the reverse: the **older** version you're downgrading to doesn't have this normalization. So when it rediscovers the socket as `//pods/...` (because [`SocketDirectoryOnHost()`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/f7ab74fe8ddb53cb2ed1d0069c3474f28eb5f672/pkg/virt-handler/cmd-client/client.go#L175-L177) didn't use `filepath.Clean()` in older versions) and compares it to the stored `/pods/...` path, it fails.

**Workaround**: For affected nodes, you can delete the ghost record checkpoint files and restart virt-handler to force rediscovery without the conflicting cached state.

The fix was backported to releases 1.0-1.6 (e.g., [release-1.6](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15367), [release-1.2](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15537)), so downgrading to any patched version should avoid this issue. Downgrades to unpatched versions with running VMIs will likely hit this problem.

**What happened**:
When a VM has a CD-ROM device with a volume attached and a container disk, ejecting the CD-ROM volume while the VM is running causes subsequent migration to fail with a "No such file or directory" error for the container disk.

**What you expected to happen**:
Migration should succeed, with container disk paths correctly resolved.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Create a VM with
   - A CD-ROM device with an occupied volume (index 0)
   - A disk (index 1)
   - A container disk (index 2)
2. Start the VM
3. Eject the CD-ROM volume while the VM is running
4. Attempt to migrate the VM

**Additional context**:

- Container disk paths are [constructed using the volume's position in the vmi.Spec.Volumes array](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/9d789083c379bf96131f7064ed0d5571806b8279/pkg/container-disk/container-disk.go#L104-L110)
- When ejecting the CD-ROM volume, the [volumes array is reindexed](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/9d789083c379bf96131f7064ed0d5571806b8279/tests/storage/declarative-hotplug.go#L161-L172) and the domain definition is regenerated with new indices. However, the physical container disk file on disk is still named `disk_2.img`. It doesn't get renamed. During migration, the target expects `disk_2.img` but it doesn't exist at that index anymore.

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): v1.7.0
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): v1.35.2
- VM or VMI specifications: will be provided later
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): N/A
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): N/A
- Install tools: N/A
- Others: N/A
", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This is a valid bug. The issue stems from an architectural limitation in how container disk paths are constructed using volume array indices.

**Root Cause**: Container disk paths are [generated using the volume's index position](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/b4591dbfaced9023ddfd29cd90dadd4b2878d97e/pkg/container-disk/container-disk.go#L104-L110) (e.g., `disk_0.img`, `disk_1.img`, `disk_2.img`). When a CD-ROM volume is ejected, the volumes array is reindexed, but:
- Physical disk files remain at their original indices on disk
- The domain definition regenerates with new indices
- [There is no logic to remount, rename, or update container disk file paths](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/b4591dbfaced9023ddfd29cd90dadd4b2878d97e/pkg/virt-handler/container-disk/mount.go#L332-L381) after ejection

During migration, [container disks are re-instantiated on the target node](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/b4591dbfaced9023ddfd29cd90dadd4b2878d97e/pkg/virt-handler/migration-target.go#L638-L651) using the current VMI spec indices, which no longer match the source.

**Related Issues/PRs**:
- [PR #16796](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16796) fixed a related CD-ROM device target naming conflict where CD-ROM and LUN devices weren't tracked in the prefix map
- [PR #15969](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15969) addressed CD-ROM detachment issues affecting volume array management
- [PR #16637](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16637) fixed decentralized live migration path mismatches between different volume modes

**Workaround**: Position CD-ROM devices at the beginning of your disk/volume list. This minimizes reindexing impact when volumes are ejected, as described in [PR #16796](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/16796).

A proper fix would likely involve either switching to name-based (rather than index-based) container disk path construction, or implementing remounting logic when the volumes array changes.

{"author": "person-c80cee2c", "body": "**What happened**:

###  Body:                                                                                                         
 
handleStaleSocketConnections in pkg/virt-handler/cache/domain-watcher.go acquires watchDogLock and then       performs a blocking send to eventChan:                                                                      
   
```go                                                                                                             
  d.watchDogLock.Lock()                                                                                       
  defer d.watchDogLock.Unlock()          // lock held for entire function                                       
  ...                                                                                                           
  d.eventChan <- watch.Event{...}         // blocks if consumer is slow                                         
  cmdclient.MarkSocketUnresponsive(key)   // RPC call also inside lock          
```                                
                                                                                                                
eventChan is buffered (size 100) but its consumer goroutine  the virt-handler reconciliation loop — can fall 
  behind during API-server calls or list/watch reconnects. When the buffer is full the send blocks. Since       
  watchDogLock is still held, any other path that tries to acquire the lock (domain cache list, other ticker    
  callbacks) will deadlock. The entire virt-handler on that node stops reconciling VMIs until the process is  
  restarted.

A secondary issue: handleResync also sends to eventChan without listening on stopChan, so the worker goroutine can block during shutdown.



@person-cb060f8c @person-f36cb5b0

**What happened**:
During a Live Migration of a Virtual Machine using Multus with Bridge CNI, the target node announces the VM's MAC address to the physical network prematurely, specifically, as soon as the target virt-launcher pod is created (during the Scheduling / PreparingTarget phases).
Since the source VM is still active and transmitting data on the source node, the physical switch detects the same MAC address on two different ports, causing MAC Flapping.

**What you expected to happen**:
The network interface on the target node should remain silent until the memory migration is finalized and the source VM is paused. The MAC address should only be visible on the target node during the final handover phase.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Steps to reproduce the behavior.

1. Setup a 2-node Kubernetes cluster with KubeVirt and Multus CNI.
2. Configure a NetworkAttachmentDefinition using the bridge CNI plugin connected to a physical bridge (L2).
3. Start a Virtual Machine with a fixed MAC address (e.g., 4a:1b:58:c2:93:07) attached to the bridge network.
4. On the target node, monitor the bridge forwarding database in real-time: `bridge monitor | while read line; do echo "[$(date '+%H:%M:%S.%3N')] $line"; done | grep -i <VM_MAC>`
5. In another terminal, monitor the migration phases: `kubectl get vmim -w`
6. Trigger a live migration: `virtctl migrate <VM_NAME>`.

**Additional context**:

```
kubectl get vmim -A -w -o custom-columns="NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,SOURCE:.status.migrationState.sourceNode,TARGET:.status.migrationState.targetNode" | while read line; do echo "[$(date '+%H:%M:%S.%3N')] $line"; done
```

Hi @person-59bcc451! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report. I can confirm your analysis - **this is a known architectural limitation** in how KubeVirt handles network setup during live migration.

**Root Cause**: The target pod's network interfaces (with the VM's MAC address) become active during the [PreparingTarget phase](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/e2a0abb64bf06ab6646e0b957057926810531dbe/pkg/virt-handler/migration-target.go#L741), **before memory migration begins**. The [nmstate adapter brings interfaces up](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/e2a0abb64bf06ab6646e0b957057926810531dbe/pkg/network/driver/nmstate/spec.go#L210-L213) immediately during network setup, making the MAC visible on the physical network while the source VM is still running.

**KubeVirt currently has no mechanism to delay network interface activation** on the target node until after migration completes.

**Important context**:
- [Live migration with bridge binding on the pod network is explicitly not supported](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/live_migration/) - this is an architectural restriction
- For secondary networks with bridge binding, [the `kubevirt.io/allow-pod-bridge-network-live-migration` annotation is required](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16386), but this doesn't solve MAC flapping

**Potential workarounds**:
1. Consider using [masquerade binding instead of bridge](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/interfaces_and_networks/) for the pod network - it supports live migration and avoids MAC exposure on physical switches
2. If you must use bridge binding on secondary networks, you may need external network coordination (e.g., via CNI plugins that delay interface activation)

I didn't find any existing issues specifically tracking this MAC flapping behavior during supported migration scenarios - **this appears to be an unreported gap**. If your configuration uses bridge on secondary networks (not pod network), filing this as a feature request for delayed network activation during migration would be valuable.

On the hardware, each separate socket corresponds to a separate NUMA node. So you would expect socket index to equal numa index but this is not true.

Of course to an extent, currently sockets are somewhat of a "cosmetic" feature. Meaning, in the KubeVirt VMI spec, you can specify:
```

      model: host-passthrough
      cores: 8
      sockets: 8
      threads: 1
```

And KubeVirt will make sure the resulting VMI says it has 8 sockets even if that does not reflect reality. While I am not sure why we allow users to specify sockets (a HW detail), I at least expect when number of sockets VMI specifies matches the actual underlying sockets, KubeVirt should reflect reality more accurately.

> Digression: Initially, when I saw this, my reaction was "OK sockets must be a scheduling constraint." Meaning I expected that if you say "sockets: 2" KubeVirt will make sure that K8 makes sure that your VMI happens to get CPUs from exactly two different sockets. Of course I realize K8 does not allow you to request CPUs with this kind of granularity.

**What you expected to happen**:
KubeVirt should opportunistically construct more accurate HW topology when possible.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Follow https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/dedicated_cpu_resources/ to enable CPUManager FG and NUMA Aware scheduling. `numa.topologyPolicy` best be `best-effort` to allow receiving CPUs from multiple sockets (assuming on this machine NUMA=sockets).
3. Ensure you requests enough CPUs to force K8 to give you CPUs from multiple NUMA nodes but in such a way that the number of CPUs from each NUMA node must be unequal. So for example, on a machine with 12 CPUs per NUMA and 2 total NUMA nodes, request 14 CPUs. This would result in getting 12 CPUs from one NUMA and 2 from the other.
4. You will observe that regardless of hardware reality, KubeVirt will evenly distribute socket information. guestMappingPassthrough must also be enabled.

Hi @person-54de13bd! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/person-43cbd26d) and I’m helping the kubevirt team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a valid observation about KubeVirt's current behavior. The socket/core/thread specification in VMI is indeed primarily about **vCPU organization** rather than accurately reflecting physical socket topology. When you specify `sockets: 2`, KubeVirt presents that topology to the guest, but it doesn't enforce that those vCPUs come from 2 physical sockets or that socket boundaries align with NUMA boundaries.

**Why this happens:**
- The [vCPU topology configuration is independent of actual hardware placement](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/virtual_hardware/) without NUMA passthrough
- KubeVirt's [numaMapping()](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/e2a0abb64bf06ab6646e0b957057926810531dbe/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/vcpu/vcpu.go#L590-L679) distributes memory and CPUs based on host NUMA boundaries, not socket boundaries
- The socket count you see in the guest is the *configured* value, not derived from actual host topology

**Closest workaround today:**
If you need topology accuracy, [NUMA GuestMappingPassthrough](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/numa/) is the mechanism that aligns guest NUMA nodes with host NUMA boundaries:

```yaml
spec:
  domain:
    cpu:
      cores: 4
      dedicatedCpuPlacement: true
      numa:
        guestMappingPassthrough: {}
    memory:
      hugepages:
        pageSize: 2Mi
```

However, this maps to **NUMA nodes**, not physical sockets. On systems where socket = NUMA node (common but not universal), this would give you accurate topology. The [documented limitation](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/numa/) is that guests may see different NUMA topologies when rescheduled, and asymmetric configurations are possible.

There's also a related [open issue (#16584)](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16584) requesting "auto" vCPU placement using libvirt's numad integration for better automatic NUMA alignment.

Your feature request for KubeVirt to opportunistically construct accurate socket topology when possible seems reasonable - essentially deriving socket values from actual pinning rather than treating them as purely cosmetic.

**What happened**:


  ### Root cause

  LibvirtDomainManager.syncDisks in pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/manager.go runs three sequential loops against
  the live libvirt domain:

  1. Detach  — calls dom.DetachDeviceFlags for each disk to remove
  2. Attach  — calls dom.AttachDeviceFlags for each disk to add
  3. Update — calls dom.UpdateDeviceFlags for each disk to remap

  None of these loops has any compensating logic. A failure at position N means items 0..N-1 are already
  committed to libvirt while N..end are not. The function returns the error immediately with no attempt to undo
  the partial work.

  Concrete failure scenarios

```
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │       Where the error occurs        │                       State left in libvirt                       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Disk B fails to detach, disk A      │ Disk A is permanently gone from the running VM                    │
  │ already detached                    │                                                                   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Disk A attaches, disk B fails to    │ Disk A is permanently attached while B is absent                  │
  │ attach                              │                                                                   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ DeleteQCOW2Overlay fails after      │ Disk is detached from libvirt but code returns an error (next     │
  │ successful detach                   │ sync sees no disk to detach, overlay leaks)                       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 3 of 5 CD-ROM updates succeed, 4th  │ Domain has 3 drives pointing at new backing file, 2 pointing at   │
  │ fails                               │ old ones                                                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

  In all cases the running guest is exposed to a device tree that no valid VM spec describes. Block I/O errors,
  guest kernel panics, and disk data corruption are all possible consequences.

**What happened**:

### Root cause                                                                                                    
  
  pkg/virt-controller/watch/migration/migration.go, case MigrationRunning :             

```go         
                                                            
  if backendstorage.IsBackendStorageNeeded(vmi) {                                                               
      err := backendstorage.MigrationHandoff(c.clientset, c.pvcStore, migration)
      if err != nil {                                                                                           
          return err   // migrationCopy.Status.Phase is still MigrationRunning
      }                                                                                                         
  }                                                                                                             
```
                                                                                                                
  MigrationHandoff patches PVC labels and deletes the source PVC. If the API server rejects the patch           
  persistently (resource quota, PVC finalizer left by a CSI driver, PVC already deleted), every reconcile
  returns the same error. Because migrationCopy.Status.Phase is never changed, the migration never leaves       
  MigrationRunning.                                         

  Consequences                                                                                                  
```  
  ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   
  │     Component      │                                    What happens                                    │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   
  │ Migration object   │ Stays in MigrationRunning forever                                                  │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   
  │ Source             │ Sees TargetNodeDomainReadyTimestamp != nil — stops considering itself              │   
  │ virt-handler       │ authoritative                                                                      │   
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   
  │ Guest              │ Paused / hung; neither node owns the domain                                        │   
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   
  │ Operator           │ No event or status change to indicate the failure                                  │
  └────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   
              
```                                              

### Suggested Fixes                                                                                   
                                                            
  1. Tracking attempt count durably on the migration object across reconcile cycles                                
  2. Enforcing a maximum before each retry

**What happened**:

On s390x, must-gather VM tests (and any VM with 2 or more network interfaces) fail to start with the following libvirt error:

```
LibvirtError(Code=1, Domain=20, Message='internal error: a PCI slot is needed to connect a PCI controller model='pcie-root-port', but none is available, and it cannot be automatically added')
```
This occurs because KubeVirt attempts to add **pcie-root-port** controllers to the VM, which is not supported on s390x (s390-ccw-virtio machine type). As a result, the VM never reaches the running state.

The recent v3 PCI topology changes introduced in 
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/17060 (release - 1.6)
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/17059 (release - 1.7)
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/17058 (release - 1.8)
unconditionally adds pcie-root-port controllers by calling the `calculatePlaceholderCount `function.

This behavior is incompatible with the s390x architecture, as PCIe hierarchy (such as pcie-root-port) is not supported. Instead, s390x uses a flat zPCI topology for PCI devices. As a result, QEMU/libvirt cannot attach a pcie-root-port controller, leading to the observed error. While s390x does support PCI devices via zPCI/CCW, it does not support adding or modeling a PCIe tree topology.


**What you expected to happen**:
VMs with multiple network interfaces (like a default masquerade and a bridge, or any extra interface) should start normally on s390x, just like they did before the v3 PCI topology changes.

This appears to be a duplicate of [#17266](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/17266), which was opened earlier today with the same issue and proposed fix.

The root cause is confirmed: the v3 PCI topology changes in [`pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/converter.go`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/d63f4afecd93264058ce8d7744a07cc4516aea3f/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/converter.go#L1147-L1151) unconditionally call `PlacePCIDevicesWithNUMAAlignment()` and create pcie-root-port controllers, but s390x uses the `s390-ccw-virtio` machine type with a flat zPCI/CCW topology rather than PCIe hierarchy.

The proposed fix from #17266 is to add an `isS390x()` helper and skip all PCIe tree/root-port/NUMA-aligned PCI placement logic for s390x at [converter.go lines 1147-1150](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/converter.go#L1147-L1150). s390x already has architecture-specific guards in other areas like [ROM tuning](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/d63f4afecd93264058ce8d7744a07cc4516aea3f/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/arch/s390x.go#L54-L57) and [PCI hole 64 disabling](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/d63f4afecd93264058ce8d7744a07cc4516aea3f/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/converter/arch/s390x.go#L72-L74), so a similar pattern can be applied here.

This is a valid bug/feature gap. **Virtctl does not support HTTP transport debugging like kubectl's `-v=9`** — the `-v` flag only controls application-level logging, not API request/response tracing.

Looking at the code:
- The [`-v` flag is registered in `client-go/log/log.go`](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/42917a864bd3ae6d090f6a20707dc1b167cad343/staging/src/kubevirt.io/client-go/log/log.go#L85-L89) and controls a go-kit logger
- [HTTP round-trippers are only wrapped for metrics collection](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/42917a864bd3ae6d090f6a20707dc1b167cad343/pkg/monitoring/metrics/common/client/rt_wrapper.go#L46-L70), not verbose logging
- kubectl achieves HTTP logging by integrating with klog's transport debugging, which virtctl hasn't implemented

Related: [Issue #16951](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/16951) reports that KubeVirt's `-v` flag registration conflicts with klog because it unconditionally registers in `init()`, unlike klog's opt-in approach. There's also an older [proposal (#5932)](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/5932) to migrate to Kubernetes structured logging.

**Workaround**: You can proxy virtctl through a debugging proxy like `mitmproxy` or use `kubectl --raw` for API calls you need to inspect.
